item.title: [a16z] Why Education Has to Change
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个反直觉的观察：这不是"新学校"，而是硅谷对"信号系统"的一次主权夺取

表面上，HA Academy 是一所面向 AI 时代的新学校。但如果你把它放在制度经济学的坐标系里看，会发现一件更有趣的事：a16z 正在自己发行"人才认证货币"。

大学四百年来真正卖的不是知识（知识早就免费了），而是信号——一种雇主可信任的排序机制。而 a16z 手握 1,600 家投资组合公司的招聘缺口，等于同时握住了信号的"发行权"和"兑付端"。这就像美联储既印钞又开银行——一旦学生毕业能被 Databricks、Stripe、Nvidia 直接吸收，"文凭"这个词的清算网络就悄悄换了一家清算所。

Ben 说"请哈佛抄我们"，这句话表面谦逊，实则是加密世界那种"开源即武器"的策略：第一个铸造出新标准的人，即使被复制，也依然是标准的锚点。

跨领域连接：这套教育模型的真正原型不是学校，而是中世纪的行会 + 硅谷的孵化器 + 日本的相扑部屋

仔细听他们描述的机制——住宿制、师徒渗透、和"成年人"共处一室、通过做真项目获得技能——这不是现代大学的形态，而是pre-industrial 的学徒制。工业革命把学徒制打碎成流水线式的班级授课，因为工厂需要标准化零件。现在 AI 把生产又推回到非标准化的个人杠杆，于是教育形态也在向后弯折——回到师徒同吃同住的"部屋"结构。

更意外的连接：Gagan 反复强调的"osmosis（渗透）"——你和什么人共处一室，你就会长成什么样——这在神经科学里叫镜像神经元耦合，在管理学里叫tacit knowledge transfer（波兰尼的隐性知识），而在日本相扑界，你几乎不通过教科书学相扑，你通过在部屋里被前辈打得鼻青脸肿来学。HA Academy 的核心赌注是：AI 时代最稀缺的不是显性知识，而是无法被 LLM 编码的隐性知识——那些只能通过身体在场获得的东西。

这也解释了一个悖论：为什么在 AI 让远程工作变得如此高效的时代，最前沿的教育机构反而要求你必须搬来旧金山？因为 AI 越强，那些不能被 AI 复制的东西——身体在场、社交气味、失败时旁边有人拍你肩膀——就越贵。

隐藏的系统性真相：他们在赌一件很少人明说的事——"精英叛逃"正在发生

Ben 说他祖父的父亲睡在缝纫机下，"未来的年轻人回望我们，就像我们回望他"。这句话被包装成励志，但它的深层假设是极其激进的：现有的整个教育-就业-信用体系，在他们看来不是"需要改良"，而是一个即将被扔进历史垃圾桶的旧世界。

这里有一个更深的系统性观察：在过去五十年里，"上大学"是美国中产阶级社会契约的核心——你付钱，你熬四年，你换来一张进入中产的门票。而 a16z 说的其实是：这个契约的兑付方（雇主）正在悄悄退出。当最好的雇主开始绕开这套系统直接从 18 岁的孩子里挑人，大学四百年积累的"信号溢价"就会开始漏气——一开始很慢，然后突然崩塌，像所有金融系统一样。

而这里有一个几乎没人指出的跨领域连接：这套逻辑和 2008 年之后加密货币兴起的动力学几乎完全同构——都是精英群体对某个"过度中介化、信用透支、既得利益盘踞"的旧系统失去耐心，用技术+资本+品牌同时铸造一个平行体系。Ben Horowitz 恰好也是加密世界最激进的支持者之一，这不是巧合。

HA Academy 本质上是"教育界的比特币"——它不需要战胜哈佛，它只需要存在，就足以让整个旧系统的定价开始被重新审视。而对个体读者而言，真正的问题不是"要不要送孩子去 HA Academy"，而是：如果这套逻辑成立，你现在正在往里面投入四年时间和三十万美元的那个东西，五年后会值多少？

📝 转录文本

为什么教育必须改变——a16z 官宣 Horowitz & Gagan Academy

开场：这是历史上最好的年轻时代

Ben Horowitz： This should be the greatest time in the history of humanity to be young. This is like Thomas Edison's time or Henry Ford's time or so forth. But the challenge that we have is everything that we've built to train you was built for a world that is soon to no longer exist.

主持人： Mark and I just commissioned this research report on Gen Z, and one of the findings was that it's the generation that has the highest variance and fragmentation across the board.

Gagan： It's critical for young people who don't have that billion-dollar idea to not settle for the million-dollar idea and instead go and explore more. We're building a new school for the AI era, and that means redesigning everything.

Ben： Let's go pursue it all and let's get an output on that.

主持人： Picture HA 5 years from now. What do you hope that we've achieved? How would you determine if we're being successful?

一、官宣：Horowitz and Gagan Academy 正式发布

主持人： Well, Ben, Gagan, we have a big announcement today.

Gagan： Yes.

主持人： We are announcing Horowitz and Gagan Academy.

Gagan： Yes we are, and we're very excited about that. Super pumped.

主持人： So let's get into the story of how how this came to be, and let's talk about what it is.

Ben, ever since I joined, you know, a year and a half ago, we've been working on bringing this to life. We found the perfect co-founder in Gagan. But you've been thinking about this at a16z for years before. So talk about what was the impetus for why we wanted to make this happen.

二、缘起：大学并不真的服务想去"做事"的孩子

Ben： Yeah, we kind of came out at it from a couple different directions.

So the first thing was — one of the things we noticed is that for young people, college works really really well if you want to be a scholar or a professor or that kind of thing. But it's a little bit of a weird proposition if you just want to get a job or you have an idea to start a company. It's a very large financial investment and a very big time investment. And most of the stuff that happens in college isn't around that. It's around other kinds of things — being a well-rounded person, this and that and the other. But if you ask an 18-year-old why do they go to college? It's to get a job usually. And that kind of doesn't always translate.

So that was one thing where we thought — you know, we've got a lot of jobs, maybe we can help with that.

And then on our side from a hiring standpoint, I think that college really evolved a lot in the last, I would say, four or five years in terms of the kind of students they're looking for and what skills they have. And in our world, the skill sets needed are evolving so fast that it was just very hard for a big system like that to keep up.

So we still think college is great for probably most kids. But there is a certain kind of kid that wants to build something, that already knows they want to go specifically currently into technology — and we have access to all the jobs, we know exactly what you need to learn, we know exactly the skills that you have to have. And so we thought, gee, that would be a great thing for us to add to the mix and provide.

三、为什么是 Gagan：十年磨一剑的创业者

主持人： And we've individually been thinking about this for over a decade. You and your many businesses, you know, having co-founded Udemy, Maven most recently. We did a search for who was the right CEO, and through the process it just became obvious that Gagan has, one, been thinking about this forever, but two, is one of the most impressive entrepreneurs in the entire space over the past decade plus.

Is there anything else you want to say about it?

Ben： Yeah, it was one of those things where we have this idea, and then we meet a guy — he's like, "You know, I've had that idea for much longer than you've had that idea. And not only that, I've spent a lot of time trying to work and make it happen — but without necessarily the gigantic resource that you guys have, which is: you're invested in 1,600 companies and you have a fairly large place of employment yourself."

And so, if you put those things together, you have the potential for something really really special.

四、为什么以前的尝试都没能突破：Bundle 才是护城河

主持人： And I think also, we as a firm have also backed many things in the space. There's a lot of people who tried to do something in the space and it hasn't really cut through. There's some interesting experiments, there's some interesting outcomes, but nothing has really taken a crack at it. And I'm curious why you guys think that is.

I'll take a stab by saying I think they focus a little bit too narrow. College is, of course, a bundle. It's a bundle of dozens of things including sports leagues and hedge fun. You don't have to do the whole bundle, but you have to do — not just training people for the job world, but also status and credential and brand. It has to be an indication that "oh, you went here, thus I want to hire you or I want to work with you." And it also has to be fun. It has to be something that people actually want to do.

And too many players just focus either just on the learning thing or just on some other hybrid, and don't create the bundle that is the value prop that is truly competitive.

Ben： Yeah. So I think that we're kind of starting out a little more specific and then we'll really ace that.

But the core idea of it is: it's for people who want to build something and do something and make an impact in the world outside of, you know, being a scholar. And to do that — be it in technology or in music or in any field — you want to learn how to do it as opposed to just study about it.

So if you think of something like music appreciation or art appreciation — that's great, but we would do the kind of thing where it's: "Oh, you want to major in music? Like, let's write some songs. Let's do some things. Let's understand that process and do that." And it's the same thing with technology — "Oh, you want to be a technologist? Let's learn how to build a system." Yeah. And I think that just ends up being very different.

五、时代切换：从工业革命到 AI 革命的教育范式转移

Ben： The other reason that now is actually the correct time to do it is: if you look at the university system, you know, it started out as this religious institution with the Jesuits and so forth. And then the industrial revolution came, and then all of a sudden everybody needed a higher level of the ability to learn things — the ability to be literate, etc. — and so the university system just exploded in the US, and the universities got much bigger and there became many more of them.

That was really necessary to train the population to enter the corporate world. It's hard for people to understand now, but in 1700 there was no corporate world. There was a farm world, and then all of a sudden we got these companies. And to exist in that environment you've got to be able to read and write and do math and this and that. So things really changed from an educational standpoint in this country, which became a huge advantage. And to a large extent, the America that we have was built on the backs of our great universities.

But we're hitting the AI revolution now, which is going to be, in our estimation, as transformational in terms of jobs, the way jobs are done, the kinds of jobs that are available and so forth, as the industrial revolution was to the agricultural society that came before it.

And the idea that the training for the industrial revolution is going to map into the AI revolution — probably not perfectly. So there needs to be a pioneer that shows the way — how do you train somebody into the new world?

And there's many things that are different. So we've got all this technology as well. Rather than being in lectures for 5 hours a day or 8 hours a day depending on your curriculum, maybe it's better to have more contained instruction and more time with the tools, more time learning on an individual pace with AI. And then also more structured social things — not necessarily "let's get rip-roaring drunk and go out" (although maybe some of that will occur too), but more structured social things, because we'll have the time — we won't have so much time sitting in the classroom listening to somebody talk.

So all these new ideas can come into play now. And the timing is, you know, for a young person now, that's the world they're going to live in.

六、Bundle 的具体设计：住宿 · 旧金山 · 雇主网络

Gagan： Yeah, I completely agree. We're building a new school for the AI era, and that means redesigning everything.

And I think that some of the other efforts don't go big enough in order to truly deliver a college-comparable experience. Obviously this is not college — it's not degree-granting — but a college-comparable experience that's good for a high school student. You have to have interpersonal social dynamics. You need to have it residential in San Francisco. You need to make sure that it's connected to the employers who employ the best people.

And so there's a bundle that's required that you have to deliver. And there's probably only two or three people who have ever even tried to deliver that bundle in the last, let's say, 50 years.

The other thing though that those companies or efforts I think missed is — it's a classic startup thing. What do you do when you start a startup? You need a very very unique specific customer who has a burning desire for your product.

And, Ben, when we first met, I hadn't met that many of these. But over the last six months, as you know, I've spent all my time with these young builders. And there is a generation of young builders who are just fired up about creating things. And that is one of the core ingredients of this academy — that they exist, and we're building it for them.

And I think that makes it different from other efforts because we have a very clear demand. And also that demand is elite. It's not demand from the far right or the far left or something where it's not perceived positively. These are the people who are going to employ hundreds of thousands of people in the future. They're going to raise a billion dollars for their company eventually. Those are the people who need our product right now, and that's what I think is really exciting.

主持人： Yeah. And students will have the opportunity — when I was in college, it was so divorced from the real world. I was interested in technology, I was reading about it, but here you're going to have access to work at companies — internet companies like Databricks, Nvidia, Stripe, dozens of others. You'll be immersed in the a16z sort of cinematic universe, that is both economic (practically from a career-oriented, very embedded in the actual work) but then also just exposure to people doing real things, interesting things — getting the osmosis of the Silicon Valley spirit.

七、如果你今天 18 岁：Ben 的建议

主持人： Ben, let's talk about — if you were 18 today, how would you be thinking about your own growth or education, learning? What's it like to be 18 today, in terms of what do you think people should be excited about? What are you nervous about?

Ben： Yeah, so I would be thrilled to be 18.

I think it is one of the best times in history to be 18. And it's unfortunate because — because of the systems for getting people into work currently, people are really nervous about their future. But if you look at it, this is like Thomas Edison's time or Henry Ford's time.

You're going into a world that only you will understand — that people like me will have a much more difficult time understanding than you will, and what's possible and what you can do. So you're going to go in at a very young age being more capable than people with 30, 40 years of experience. And that's just amazing.

Because normally you've got to work your way up the corporate ladder — spend 20 years developing your status and credibility — whereas now you can come out right off the rip using the new tools to basically solve almost any problem out there.

And the funny thing is, well, what are people going to do? It's like — are we out of problems? It seems like we have — all I read about is problems. There's problems everywhere. So now you can go out and attack them directly, either yourself as the leader or as part of a team. But that to me is the thing that's really really exciting.

一个家族史的比喻

And I heard a lot about the industrial revolution transition — because my grandfather's father immigrated the family out of Russia because they were going to kill all the Jews. So they had to leave — it was the pilgrim period. And he basically was a slave here, in that he was in a sweatshop. He slept under his sewing machine because he worked so many hours. He'd slept at the office under his sewing machine. He'd come back on the weekends. And he made very little money — it was a very very hard life for him.

But my grandfather was able to get an education at CCNY and became a teacher and had a much better life. Although it was also not nearly as good as my father's, who was the next generation coming out of it.

And I think for this, when we look back, I think the young people today will look at us and their parents as though you guys were sleeping under sewing machines — pretty bitter compared to what's going to be possible.

So it's a very very exciting time. But you want to be on the right side of history and you want to be future forward. I think the past is going to fade very fast — much faster than we're used to.

八、经验、关系、进大厂："即便建东西很容易"

主持人： Talk about how, even though it's so easy to build, you still want to have experience, relationships, connections — spend some time at some of these iconic companies. Because when you're just a kid, you might think "oh, I want to start a dating app idea or pizza idea," but if you work at Databricks for a bit, say, as an example — talk a little bit about that.

Ben： Yeah. So if you're young and you see something that you go, "Oh my god, I think I'm the only one who really understands this, and it's compelling me to build a company," then that's phenomenal — that's Mark Zuckerberg, that's an unbelievable opportunity, but also a rare one.

And then I think most people who are young — or the majority — would love to understand that thing. And by the way, all of Zuck's roommates from Harvard who didn't go to Facebook with him really regretted that — because he kind of invited them all to be employees, and many of them didn't do it. And they're like, "Dagnabbit, that would have been so exciting."

So there's a great opportunity to join up with people who have done that kind of thing — either something that's further along (depending on if you really want to learn and develop your skills) or maybe one of your classmates is doing something really exciting, like in the case of Facebook at the time.

So there are plenty of opportunities depending on how powerful your new ideas are at that time. And sometimes they're not that powerful. I didn't have a great idea when I was 18. So it's not that common. It took me a while to learn — I'm not as quick as others on that, I guess.

But if you get in — the great thing for me is I got in at a company, Silicon Graphics, which had all kinds of innovation, and I saw what that was and how you can really change things. And that built a foundation for the rest of my career.

九、People Skills：怎么在 18 岁学"人"

主持人： We always talk about builder skills but also people skills. You've written a couple of books on it. You talk about it all the time internally. Is that something you knew when you were 18 or in college, or how do you learn people skills? How should we teach it to our students?

Ben： Well look, I think the main thing is to be around people.

People often talk about, particularly the millennial generation, having this loneliness epidemic because they're so locked into their screens. I think one of the things that AI has the potential to do is just get us off the screen. We're not that far away from "I'm going to talk to my AI and have him do the work and deal with the dang computer." And so that's going to free me up to really deal with people, where there's going to be tremendous value — being able to know my peers, motivate them, get the best out of each other, do something larger than ourselves and try to move the future forward and make the world a better place.

So getting experience in that environment where you're working with others and learning — "Hey, yeah, I mean" — college, by the way, has been great for this over the years, where you're like, "Oh, you come from Nebraska. I never knew anybody from Nebraska. Like, what is it like? Is it just cornfields?" And you get to know people.

And probably one of the skills that I see missing the most — which I try to impart in people on the firm — is: let's just start with who the person you're talking to is. Rather than just talking to somebody, "Hey Eric, how you doing?" — like, where'd you grow up? Where are you from? Oh, that's interesting. You've got this parent from this place, this other parent from the other place — that's really good, what was that like? How did they get along?

And then you start to understand people. And that opportunity in a business context isn't as obvious if you haven't. But you always do that when you get with a group of kids your age — that's the first thing you ask them. You want to know: do you get along with your parents? You hate your parents? That kind of thing.

Osmosis：靠"泡"出来

Gagan： Yeah, one of the most important things we want is to develop people's skills. And one of the core tenets of developing a skill like that is osmosis. You need to immerse the student in the social environment in which the humans are.

And specifically, I think it's a challenge if you go off to college — you only interact with people your same year. You finally maybe have a friend who's one or two years above you or below you.

One of the things I think the Academy will do is: we obviously want there to be deep social networks amongst your peers. We also are going to try and cohabitate you, especially in the office, with other companies and individuals and projects and co-ops and internships that are with the "adult world" — so that you have no choice.

Like, if you're trying to accomplish — let's say you're trying to build a new type of robot dog, and the only way to do it is to get a specific type of chip, and you don't know how to write a cold email — you're going to have to learn. And you're going to have all these people around you who are experts at this. So they're going to be like, "Oh, you should do that, you should do that."

I think that the combination of the osmosis of Silicon Valley, a peer network that's supportive, and a project-based curriculum combined will dramatically accelerate people's skill development — over something like: let me sit in a lecture talking about negotiations. That's not how you develop people's skills. You develop people's skills because you're doing something you really care about and you need to get everyone on board.

Gen Z 的变异性最大化

主持人： Yeah, 100%. Related — Mark and I just commissioned this research report on Gen Z. And one of the findings was that it's the generation that has the highest variance and fragmentation across the board. So any subculture — they're the most extreme at it.

For example, back when we were in college, it was rare to have an 18-year-old who was already building startups, immersed in the startup world, obsessed with this kind of thing. And now there are a bunch of them, and we're going to harness them.

But to your point, Ben, it's important — the people you surround yourself with. And so now it's higher variance than ever to find your people — people who are builders, resilient, entrepreneurial. Being able to aggregate them in the same place is just huge.

Gagan： Yeah, we're really excited. I've been so impressed by the talent that we've had a chance to meet. I mean, I didn't know a single person who was doing anything entrepreneurial when I was a child, and I started my first venture at 13. So the idea that we're going to collect 50 — in at least in the founding class fellowship, 50 students — who are all actually builders, and they're going to be different kinds of builders (I want to be clear this'll be quite a broad definition of the word "building"), but all in one place, and for them to meet each other and spend a bunch of time riffing off each other — I'm very excited about it.

十、为什么必须在加州、在旧金山

主持人： Let's talk about the importance of this being in California, in the extended Bay Area. Ben, you grew up in Berkeley.

Ben： Republic. Absolutely.

主持人： Yes, exactly. Which at the time was like 10,000 miles from Silicon Valley — even though it was only like a half-hour drive.

Ben： Yeah.

主持人： And I think it's so interesting — because you grew up in California, so you know that it's not just a technical bastion but also a cultural bastion, intellectual bastion. It's so interesting because we're focused largely on the builder element first, but people say college is for building a career, but also becoming, you know, pursuing knowledge and becoming a better person. Talk about why California — and specifically San Francisco — is just such an important place for this to be. What is the opportunity here?

Ben： Well, I think the big thing is: it's where most great companies in America get started. And then America is one of two places in the world where a giant number of companies get started. So everybody who has done that and knows how to do that — a huge majority — are here in California. So if you want to learn how to do that, or if you want to go work with people who do that, then it's the most obvious place to put it.

And look, I went to college in New York. Most of the people who came out of academia went into financial services — that was the main employer, the main recruiter there.

And for a program like this, we're connected to so many companies — but well over 80% of them are right in this area. So it just makes it very convenient. You come here, you learn the area, and guess what? You can start your career right in that place.

校园就是城市

Gagan： Yeah, San Francisco is your campus. The campus is not just the walls within the school, but the entire city. And I think that's very important.

The other thing I'll add is that if San Francisco is the campus, the cultural values of San Francisco — that many people don't talk about... San Francisco is one of the places that embraces failure. If things don't work out, we'll still fund your next company. Silicon Valley is one of the places that's positive-sum. Everyone believes that if I help someone, I don't need to get anything in return — I'm going to pay it forward, and I know it's going to come back to me, because that's the culture we live in. It's a super high-trust culture.

So I think that it's going to create a really really calm, safe, and positive environment for students that is also super ambitious. It's a rare combination. It's very hard to get right. And I think Silicon Valley and San Francisco in particular really has figured that out.

主持人： I think another way of phrasing it is: if you want a stake in the future — if you want to help determine it, help argue it, help build it — a lot of it happens in San Francisco. Whether it's the future of art, AI, whether it's the future of money, whether it's the future of biotech — so many of these technologies, but also the conversations surrounding those technologies, are litigated here or started here and then expanded out that way.

Ben： And litigated here.

主持人： Yes. Both metaphorically and literally.

十一、为什么是独立公司、为什么必须是营利实体

主持人： Ben, talk about the decision to make this a separate company. We went back and forth on this for a while — why Horowitz and Gagan Academy — we wanted it to both be separate but also connected. That's why we kept the brand the same, and also it has to be a strong brand that signals to students. But talk about that decision a little bit, and how you see it interfacing with the firm at large.

Ben： Yeah. So the thing that the firm brings that's extremely unique is: we are comprehensively connected to basically every opportunity in tech. And we're working to make those partnerships explicit around the graduates of the Academy — if you go through this program, if you do well, there are many opportunities for you. That was the real strength that we brought, I thought.

But this is its own idea. We're an investment firm — this is not an investment idea. I mean, it's an investment in the future of the country, but it's an academy, which we're not. And so it really needed to be separate and have its own [identity].

In addition, I don't think that this idea is limited to technology. As I said, I think it's very interesting for music. It may be interesting for medicine. It could be interesting for a variety of things, because every profession is undergoing a massive change. And so we wanted it to be able to grow and expand as we got it working. It didn't make sense to be a piece of the firm — that would have limited its ambition quite a bit. And we're not about limiting ambition around here.

学生是唯一的客户

主持人： Totally. And talk about why it had to be a for-profit — or put differently, another thing we said in previous conversations: the customer has got to be the student. And right now, sometimes in certain institutions, they try to serve too many customers, and it kind of ends up being this disjointed product.

Ben： Yeah. So look, the whole thing is: if you're young — it goes back to our earlier conversation — if you're young, this should be the greatest time in the history of humanity to be young. But the challenge that we have is: everything that we've built to train you was built for a world that is soon to no longer exist.

So somebody's got to super-serve that client.

And look, I think my hope is that as we show this model, as we build this model, as we create it — we're not the only ones that will have it. This isn't an idea where we're going, "Okay, we're going to create a monopoly on this thing." It's like: no, please copy us. Please Harvard, copy us. Please everybody, copy us. Because somebody's got to do the innovative work to get the breakthrough — but then that's going to change the world for every young person in this country, and maybe beyond.

So that's the idea. We don't care about serving the alumni or serving the donors or serving the parent. This is about the young people — what do they need, and what's going to create the best life for them. And so that simplifies the equation quite a bit.

Gagan： Yeah. The profit motive forces us to deliver to the customer. And our job at the end of the day is to make sure that young people who attend the institution go off and do great things — because that creates the brand, that creates the flywheel that allows us to continue to stay in business. And I think that's very unique in education, that we have such incentive alignment. I think it's a core tenet, actually, of the Academy.

十二、好奇心作为教学核心：从"填桶"到"点火"

主持人： Yeah, similarly — one of the core tenets of the Academy is curiosity. And there's this quote: "Education is not the filling of a bucket, but the lighting of a fire."

We're moving from this "push" model — the grades and all this stuff you have to cram — to this "pull" — what are you naturally curious about, and what can you go build or pursue in that space? And it may not be obvious all the time what it will lead to.

We were talking about how Steve Jobs had this interest in calligraphy, and that didn't seem like it would obviously lead to anything, but in fact it led to quite a lot.

And similarly, Ben, you've always been interested in rap music.

Ben： Yes.

主持人： And you were pursuing your interest at a very young age.

Ben： I still am. Yeah.

主持人： Exactly. And it maybe wasn't obvious at the time how that might lead to something, but it's made you much more authentic and interesting as a business person and made your life...

Ben： And a better storyteller — which is a key part of what I do.

主持人： And that's definitely important in the context of the Academy and what we're trying to do — in terms of, yeah, let's go pursue it all. But then let's get an output on that.

Not — much more oriented around "oh, did you build something interesting" than "oh, could you memorize these questions." Because look, we do have tools that can answer those questions very well now.

Dan Boneh 的两难：要么禁 AI，要么把题目变到没 AI 就做不出

It's funny. I was talking to Dan Boneh, who is a great professor of computer science at Stanford — cryptography. And his take on AI was: you have two choices. You can ban it — and by the way, that won't work. Or you can make the problems so hard that you can't solve them without AI.

And I think his orientation is amazing there. And what he's seeing is: "Oh, I've got students solving things that no student in history could have ever solved — that I couldn't even solve myself."

But that's what's possible, right? So you want to have that orientation where it's like — well, what can you solve with the tools, and what can you do that's breakthrough? Because now everybody's got an opportunity to create a breakthrough. And that's super exciting.

Because then you're a main character, not an NPC, right? That's what the Academy is about — like, hey, do you want to be a main character? If you want to be a main character, we help you do that. If you want to be a cog in a machine, then this is not going to be the best place for you — but there are many places that can serve that.

用 Builder 心态去学任何东西——哪怕是书法

Gagan： Yeah. And I think it's important that the builder mentality apply to interests that are not obviously about AI or building.

So take calligraphy for example. You know, it's one thing to say, "Hey, why don't you go study calligraphy" and respond and answer questions on a test about how to — I know nothing about calligraphy — how to draw beautiful letters.

And it's another thing to say: "Hey, why don't you learn enough calligraphy to write an Islamic poem, beautifully displayed in the Academy?"

And so for every pursuit that we — Ben, you earlier talked about music — for every pursuit of knowledge that our students have, we are going to reframe that into: how do you do something with it? Create a challenge, a project, anything that's fun and interesting that allows you to go pursue it.

And I think that ethos will allow them to learn skills that are not relevant to jobs obviously — like even horticulture, or learning how to kite surf, whatever it is — but it allows them to do it in a way that ensures that they actually learn the skill. It's very very hard to learn most skills if all you're doing is cramming for a test.

十三、内在游戏：CEO 是练出来的，不是读出来的

主持人： On the people skills, there's a few different dimensions. Some people make the analogy — you know, founder is like being a movie director. You've got to create script, bring all the actors involved, and then make it happen. Other people compare it to a nightclub promoter — you have to get people excited about things, you have to bring them in, you have to sell, you have to negotiate.

At the same time, there are people who are charismatic, but also crash out. And, Ben, you talk a lot about the inner game of managing your own psychology. You've worked with — you still work with — a lot of very idiosyncratic people. So, how do you as a kid learn this? What might you say there?

Ben： Well, look. I think that's, again, difficult to teach in a classroom.

And here's the thing that I always tell CEOs — and a lot of them read my book, so I don't want to — but that book doesn't teach you how to be a CEO in the sense that... you can read every book ever written on how to play football. But if you get into an NFL game and you're playing quarterback, nothing in a book is going to teach you to deal with some 300-pound monster rushing at you while you're trying to figure out who to throw the ball to. You actually have to do that in order to learn it.

You kind of have to do it to learn it. And so a lot of what we're going to orient the Academy about is: okay, can you put a team together? Can you do it?

And there'll be less on the line — it'll be more like practice than the game. But that's the way you learn that decision-making. What does it cost you if you hesitate on the decision? What does it mean to not resolve a conflict? What are the consequences?

You can read about that. And I can tell you about that. But until you know that feeling — that horrible feeling — you're not really going to learn it to the level that you need to run a company.

十四、如果今天 18 岁，怎么选方向？

主持人： To that end — because the tools are so good, our resources are so good, it's easier than ever to do something once you know what you want to do. And so the constraint often comes on: what's worth working on? How do you spend your time? If you were 18 today — because there's so many different trade-offs — how would you think about it?

Ben： Well, I think a lot of it comes down to what you're interested in, what your skill set matches, and what's some problem that you know about that you can solve.

There's so many diseases that are so destructive. There's all kinds of challenges with the environment. There's real challenges in the integrity of our election system. Is there a technological answer to that? Or is there just a systems answer? And so on and so forth — depending on what problem you're like, "Dang, we need to fix that."

And then, by the way, what always happens with entrepreneurs — it's kind of like scientific discovery. You go to fix... you're like, "We're going to go get a cure for pancreatic cancer," but along the way you find, "Oh no, we can solve this other thing that's also important, because we discovered something there." Most scientific discoveries and entrepreneurial ideas end up being accidental in some way — that you're going to solve a hard problem, and you find some other hard problem that's in the way of you solving that hard problem, that ends up being the thing that becomes the idea.

And that's why I believe it's critical for young people who don't have that billion-dollar idea to not settle for the million-dollar idea, and instead go and explore more.

Gagan： Yeah. A lot of young people are not yet exposed to anything beyond what a teenage life includes. And one of the real core values of the Academy is: we're going to expose you to a much wider range of what happens in the real world.

硅谷所说的"拥抱失败"到底是什么意思

Ben： And look — to try and fail at a really hard problem, the value is in the learning. So people say, "Oh, Silicon Valley embraces failure." Well, not all kinds of failure. The failure where you learn a tremendous amount, and then you've earned a secret. By going out there trying to solve a hard problem and not being able to — now you know why that problem's so hard to solve. Okay, so then what are the subproblems, and what are the related problems, and can you solve one of those?

And that knowledge that you earn by failing is what we value here. And that's the same kind of thing that we would value at the Academy — like, what did you learn by doing?

十五、五年后的 HA：成功长什么样

主持人： Yeah. Picture HA five years from now. What do you hope that we've achieved? How would you determine if we're being successful? Talk about what you envision.

Ben： Well, I think in five years there are many things that would make it a success.

One is that we have graduates who have great careers that they love, or have started really interesting companies. Maybe they probably wouldn't be successful in that time frame, or whatever you consider a success.

And that we've learned, as the Academy, what really works — and can we extend that and expand that so we can get more different kinds of students in? Maybe not just: okay, technology is interesting to you — but you're really interested in these other things. And get people who can solve all the problems of the world, or become incredible creatives.

And the creative world is changing too. Now, when I talk to my creative friends, they're like: "It's amazing, because I have an idea about a feeling that I want to convey — and I can absolutely do it in every medium now. I'm not just restricted to my thing. I can make a full-length feature film. I can make a movie. I can make a song. I can score a movie."

And so now, like, everything is possible. And so I think it's just a wonderful time to be able to manifest your ideas and get your ideas out in every kind of medium. And we want to facilitate that across the board — not just in our traditional lanes.

主持人： Well, it's going to be incredible to build that future out with both of you and all the students who join us.

Ben： All right.

Gagan： So excited. Yeah, very excited.

主持人： Thank you.

表面上，HA Academy 是一所面向 AI 时代的新学校。但如果你把它放在制度经济学的坐标系里看，会发现一件更有趣的事：**a16z 正在自己发行"人才认证货币"**。
大学四百年来真正卖的不是知识（知识早就免费了），而是**信号**——一种雇主可信任的排序机制。而 a16z 手握 1,600 家投资组合公司的招聘缺口，等于同时握住了信号的"发行权"和"兑付端"。这就像美联储既印钞又开银行——一旦学生毕业能被 Databricks、Stripe、Nvidia 直接吸收，"文凭"这个词的清算网络就悄悄换了一家清算所。

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

隐藏的系统性洞察

意外观察：这不是一个 AI 公司的故事，而是一个"人类知识液态化"的故事

大多数人听 Gabe 的访谈，会把 Rogo 理解为"金融领域的 Harvey"或"投行的 ChatGPT"。但真正的隐藏叙事在他不经意的一句话里："你要开始把最优秀的人脑中那些潜在的东西，装进你自己拥有和运营的系统里。" 这句话的颠覆性在于——他描述的不是效率工具，而是一场关于"人力资本所有权"的世纪级转移。

过去 200 年，投行和对冲基金的核心资产是"关系"和"直觉"，这些资产寄生在人脑里，会跟着人跳槽而流失（想想 2008 年后美林向摩根士丹利的人才大迁徙）。Rogo 本质上是在提供一种"知识产权固化技术"——把明星银行家的隐性知识从"随时可能离职的碳基载体"中蒸馏出来，注入到"雇主拥有的硅基载体"中。这与其说是软件生意，不如说是劳动关系史上的一次相变。你会发现 Gabe 内部工具叫"Shrek"、强制记录所有对话、公开羞辱 AI 使用率最低的员工——这些不是管理风格，是知识殖民的仪式化过程。

跨领域连接：Rogo 与 17 世纪伦敦劳埃德咖啡馆

这里有个让人意外的历史平行：Gabe 说他要做的不是 Bloomberg 终端，而是"agent 之间交易的通讯层"——让 KKR 的 agent 和 Apollo 的 agent 互相谈判、拍卖资产。

这精确地重演了 1688 年伦敦的 Lloyd's Coffee House。当时爱德华·劳埃德的咖啡馆之所以变成全球保险中心，不是因为咖啡好，而是因为它偶然成为了"船长、船东、投机者之间的高带宽通讯协议"。协议标准化了——语言、单据、信任机制——于是保险市场从"熟人握手"变成了流动的资本市场。

Gabe 说的"标准化让私募市场变得像公募市场一样流动"，实际上是在赌一场"劳埃德时刻的重演"——只不过这次，坐在咖啡馆里喝咖啡的不再是人，而是数千个 agent。这里的隐藏含义很尖锐：如果历史押韵，那么 Rogo 的终极形态既不是软件公司也不是投行，而是"agent 时代的清算所"（clearinghouse）——一种主权级的市场基础设施。这也解释了为什么他敢说 500 亿美元收入不够，要奔着"重塑资本市场"去。

反常识的系统性真相：他最害怕的不是竞争，是"人类的顾问依恋"

节目里 Gabe 最含糊、最欲言又止的地方，是被问到"什么最不确定"时的回答——他谈的不是 OpenAI，不是监管，而是："20 年建立起来的小企业主，愿不愿意点个按钮把公司卖掉，而不是握个手。"

这暴露了一个反直觉的真相：在 AI 全面取代认知劳动的世界里，"最难被自动化的"不是分析能力，而是"仪式性信任"（ritualized trust）——那些看起来低效、感性、非理性的握手、晚宴、私人介绍。

这里有个跨领域连接：这跟婚姻介绍所的困境是同一个问题。Match.com 早就能用算法比任何红娘更精准地匹配伴侣，但为什么高端相亲市场仍然依赖人肉红娘？因为人类在做"存在级决策"（existential decisions）时，需要的不是准确性，而是"可归责的仪式"——一个可以埋怨、可以感谢、可以在事后叙事的具体对象。

这给 Rogo 提出了一个哲学难题：它可能能自动化 99% 的金融流程，但那最后的 1%——"我把毕生心血卖给谁"——本质上是一个抗算法的领域。 这也解释了为什么 Gabe 反复强调"公司大脑"（Shrek）——他真正在建的护城河不是 AI 能力，而是在 agent 世界里替客户扮演"值得托付的人"的能力。这是一个奇怪的定位：一个用极致技术手段来复制"人性温度"的商业实体。这或许才是所有垂直 AI 公司的终极战场——谁能最优雅地伪装成"仍然有人在关心你"。

📝 转录文本

一、开场：模型比我认识的所有人都聪明

Gabe：What we're seeing right now though is the models are smarter than anyone I know, anyone I spend time with.

Imagine if every PM at a hedge fund had 10,000 agents that were just kind of fraternizing, talking about ideas, reading through the notes, pontificating, and then at the end of, you know, 24 hours of endless debate just gave you one idea.

In 10 years, the world's best investment firms, best banks will have 90% of their enterprise value, not in people, but in software and data and systems. What would you start doing? You would start trying to figure out how do you take all of what lives in the latent minds of your best people and putting it into a system that you own and operate. There's no part of the business that you hold sacred that is immune to being revolutionized.

二、投资超级智能的两年 vs 十年

Patrick：You and I have talked many times about this basic question that I'll start with. Over the last couple of years, you're effectively trying to build investing super intelligence tools to help investors do their job much faster, better, cheaper, easier, higher quality. But it's starting to feel like, wow, we're really eating a lot of the core functions that even a very smart analyst or even portfolio manager was doing a couple years ago. How do you think about that trajectory as you've seen it and lived it so far, and where it's going over the next two years?

Gabe：I think two years is actually easier to reason about than 10 years or 20 years, because in two years the best investors are going to be figuring out how to reinvent their own firms and reinvent themselves.

If you look at what happened to market making and quant trading — Jane Street took 15 years to build the dominant franchise. And the world's best investors today are going to spend the next 2 to 5 years figuring out how to integrate AI into what they do.

Dario has the great line about everyone's going to have a data center full of geniuses or a country full of geniuses in the data center. What would Goldman do? What would Millennium do? What would Citadel do if they had a country full of geniuses show up? It would probably take them a while to figure out how to change the way they work, how to take advantage of that, how to integrate it into their system.

I think figuring out how to apply AI into the investment life cycle is the biggest challenge over the next 5 years for every great investor.

三、Rogo 的三个纪元：从"魔法演示"到"真的能用"

Patrick：There's been many companies on this trajectory — Cognition is famous for their ads now saying "remember Devon like it's good now." Lots of now clearly great companies had a stage where the product stunk and now it's excellent. Could you do the same thing for the eras of Rogo?

Gabe：I actually tried starting Rogo two times before we got started.

  • 高中时代：a friend whose dad was an investment banker wanted an app for tracking the equity exchange rate of two public companies as they were merging. We tried using really old AI techniques. Terrible.
  • 大学时代 (pre-GPT-3)：published a paper on AI assistance for econometrics and financial econometrics. Tried commercializing — nothing worked at all.
  • 真正的起点 (GPT-3 时代, pre-ChatGPT)：In the early days of Rogo, it was clear how kind of magical it was. You could demo things that were cool. Nothing worked at all.

I would say since things actually started to work, the eras are very tied to the model eras:

  • o1 Pro：the first time you got enough reliability where it was a good search tool at the very least. You could say "help me calculate this financial metric for this business over the last 12 quarters" and it could do it reliably enough where it wasn't so annoying that you would just do it yourself.
  • Opus 4.5 (end of 2025 → early 2026)：the models just became capable of basically anything a junior investment professional or junior banker was doing, as long as you gave it the right instructions and context.

There was a first mover's disadvantage for a lot of applied AI companies — you thought you knew where the world was going, the models weren't quite there, people tried it and went "this is terrible, this is garbage." But if you were right about the end state, when the models get there, it's magical.

People all day are saying: "Hey, this is transforming the way I work. I'm saving hundreds of hours a month. I am doing things I never could have done before. I'm smarter as a result. And it's delightful — the UX and the attention to detail and the craftsmanship is so obviously built for me."

四、"iPad + 邮件"：为不登录电脑的董事总经理设计

Patrick：You took seriously all the compliance, regulatory workflow, last mile hookup stuff — and then the models became good enough and suddenly that was super valuable.

Gabe：There's also small details of understanding how someone within one of these firms works and building for it.

举个例子：We make it so easy for a managing director at a bank to email a markup of a deck (which is how they're typically doing these workflows anyway) — except sending it to our AI analyst over email, and returning that markup in 20 minutes as opposed to 2 days. At the same time, alert the junior analyst on the deal, show them the full auditability of all the little markups that were made in case they want to weigh in.

That whole UX makes it so much easier for a financial professional who is not logged into a computer in 10 years, but does have an iPad where they know how to mark these things up.

五、前沿：一万个 agent 只为一个想法

Patrick：What is the bleeding edge of what it can do that impresses you the most?

Gabe：The coolest things we're working on is taking innovations like Multbook. Imagine if every PM at a hedge fund had 10,000 agents fraternizing, talking about ideas, reading through the notes, pontificating, and then at the end of 24 hours of endless debate just gave you one idea.

And the reason you're able to do that is because investors are happy to pay $50,000 for one really good idea. There's very few other domains where you can expend that many tokens just for one simple insight.

What we're seeing right now is that the models are smarter than anyone I know. And it's plumbing — connect it to your context, inform it about your thesis, tell it the way that you work, integrate it into what you do. Building out all the plumbing to actually collect that data, that context, is what is cutting edge to me.

六、周一早上：谁在使用 Rogo？

Patrick：If I adopted a god's eye view of a Monday morning here in New York City — lots of Rogo users are probably fired up right now. Who are the people? What are the predominant use cases?

Gabe：Even though in so many ways I think public equities is the best application of AI (because all the data is available), our early users and core ICP is what I would describe as dealmakers — people transacting, buying companies, selling companies, coordinating transactions.

We both make people smarter and actually do the dealmaking: - How do you prepare a data room? - How do you unpack a data room? - How do you coordinate the call with the third parties? - How do you go through all of the initial steps through closing of a deal?

If you took a bird's eye view of all the folks using Rogo, it's people who are either on the sell side of a transaction or the buying side, using it to prepare all the thoughts and materials to help execute the full deal.

冰山之下的另一半：Rogo is actually in a lot of the behind-the-scenes systems — CRM, portfolio and monitoring systems, LP distribution. Half of our surface area is the underneath of the iceberg — interacting with these different systems of record based on what the humans are doing.

七、为什么先做私募而不是公募

Patrick：When do you think you'll be able to give the same answer for junior analysts at a public equity hedge fund?

Gabe：For our business, we need to have all the requisite domain knowledge of what it takes to be a great public markets investor. I don't know what it takes. I've never done it.

I get pushed a lot by our board to think about expanding the ICP beyond just core banking, but there's been so much depth in TAM in this dealmakers vertical.

For my end-state vision — being the full infrastructure for private markets where people can transact very effectively — that is far more important. Whereas for public equities, all that infrastructure, all those exchanges already exist.

关键洞察：

A lot of the opportunity to build an AI business in a vertical is somewhere where there's lots of plumbing that's not yet built. Private markets are so attractive because it's all done by humans — the coordination, the standardization, the actual transacting. Whereas in public equities, a lot has been automated.

八、未来投资人还需要什么技能？

Patrick：What the hell are we going to do if the thing can do the soup-to-nuts diligence and IC memo and objection handling?

Gabe：The world's best investors have a way of figuring out what matters and exercising their own judgment across a range of topics. Jury is still out on whether that is something AI can eventually replace.

When Move 37 happened and Lee Sedol saw something he could never see — if that starts to happen in public equities, it's going to really change what matters.

I think the core skill set is folks who can go out and gather data and inputs into their model that no one else will have. If you can spend time in the field, if you can speak to experts, if you can develop a relationship graph — maybe you're not the one calculating what your Move 37 would be, but you can feed your model with data no one else has.

[广告：Ramp、Rogo、WorkOS]

九、装配线：数据、模型、还是 Harness？

Patrick：Tell me about the entire system — data, models, how it's evolved.

Gabe：The early days of Rogo was this Rube Goldberg contraption where you had 60 different model calls. A question comes in, try to say what companies is Patrick asking about, now what are their tickers, feed those into an API call to Bloomberg or FactSet, comes back, call a different model to pull it all together.

As the models get smarter, you want to be less prescriptive, less of a Rube Goldberg machine, and just think about: what are the simplest, best, highest quality tools?

Same way that if you have the world's smartest human being starting tomorrow trying to be a great banker and investor — what tools would they need? - 数据工具 - 收集信息的方式 - 审计自己工作的方式 - 呈现并推回系统的方式

We also spend a lot of time on compliance and regulatory: if someday some Delaware court judge makes AI inputs and research discoverable, you've done it all the right way. The reality of AI investment judgments is that you're going to be able to see the full lineage of how those things are created.

We spend a lot of time benchmarking these models and creating different evals so we can decide what is the most performant, the cheapest from a token perspective, the lowest latency — and route tasks to the appropriate type of models.

十、如何与 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 竞争？

Patrick：I'm sure your favorite question is: how do you ultimately compete with Anthropic and OpenAI who view finance as a big category?

Gabe：You want to build things that are perpendicular to what they want to build. Sometimes you might build a chatbot because that helps you go to market faster, but you should know there's a whole bunch of stuff underneath the surface that the labs are never going to build.

When you think about financial services and capital markets, how many businesses are there that generate more than $5 or $10 billion by just going deep into those workflows? All of finance is a collection of different niches with different data sets, different definitions of good, different regulatory requirements. We can get to $5 billion in revenue by going deep across those things and creating the systems of record.

For Anthropic, that would kind of be like stopping on the side of the road to pick up a penny, because they're on the pathway of trying to go from $100 billion to a trillion in revenue.

具体例子 1：MNPI 合规 If you are ingesting MNPI because you're working on transactions — the compliance requirements just in auditability, what you can flag, how it feeds into internal systems. If you ever get audited or a regulator wants to see what you did, do you have all that plumbing in place that is pixel-perfect?

具体例子 2：Data Room If a big public company is buying another and you need to send data back and forth — you need some sort of data room that's compliant, safe, secure, coordinates, and ideally plugged into the way you do work. I don't think OpenAI or Anthropic will ever want to build a data room business.

If you actually want to be the exchange for all of high finance and capital markets, you not just need to own the intelligence — you need to own the transaction venue, the communication venue, the workflows, and all the data inputs.

十一、Harness 的重要性被严重低估

Patrick：It sounds like harness or infrastructure is probably the most important of the three.

Gabe：Think about the fundamental difference between Claude Code and OpenAI's ChatGPT. The models were actually fairly similar, but the harness and the way that it was presented from Claude was far better. It allowed the models to exercise more of their long-running capabilities.

People underappreciate that intelligence — the reasons humans are high-agency isn't just raw recall and IQ, but all these different microservices in your brain. How do you put knowledge away? How do you retrieve it? How do you trigger things? Emotions are a way to trigger these microservices.

A great investor might have great judgment because they have a good spidey sense — when they see this sort of thing in the market, it actually triggers the recall from this event that informs a creative decision.

十二、投资一家 Rogo-like 公司会看什么？

Gabe： 1. 行业本身要有足够的复杂性和深度 — 数据类型、系统记录、部署模式，让你能花大量精力解决这些问题，形成 wedge。如果一个行业任何人都能走进去卖基础版 ChatGPT，你就没有足够时间构建那些垂直的东西。 2. 团队的行业专业性。I don't have unique domain expertise, but I had enough to get started. And then I was so curious about finance and money and capital markets. We assembled a team uniquely passionate about it — over a hundred people who have spent time within investment banks or investment firms. 3. 愿意不断重造核心产品，愿意把它砍到什么都不剩。像 Max Levchin 讲的 Affirm 每年重建底层账本技术 —— it's the most interesting engineering problem, so engineers want to work on it, and it keeps the system from ossifying.

十三、模型还不能做的事：Compaction（记忆压缩）

Patrick：What's something that the models currently cannot do that would really change the nature of the product?

Gabe：Compaction. If you have 100 conversations with a single agent, how does it make sure it's remembering the right things and compacting its memory into an amount of tokens it can use every time, with enough coherence and context on who you are and what you care about?

It compounds exponentially when agents aren't just one-to-one — right now almost all agents are one-to-one (ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini individually). As soon as these are things that consort with a lot of colleagues, or in a Slack channel with 100 people, or work across an entire company — the compaction problem scales exponentially.

十四、企业软件 vs. Token 消费模式

Patrick：What kind of category would you put Rogo in? Usage-based? Seat-based?

Gabe：We are a classic enterprise software business. We price per seat right now because our buyers are used to it. They think of us similar to Bloomberg, FactSet, Capital IQ, Pitchbook.

We have to build a very human business. Every time you sign a deal, it requires an AE, solutions architect, sales engineer going in shaking hands. You can't sign one deal where usage rises 100-fold.

Compare: how hard it was for Anthropic to sell to us? Very easy. And the amount we pay them has risen exponentially without a human in the loop — because it's a token consumption model.

We have to build a go-to-market machine five times faster than most enterprise sales organizations ever have to build.

未来的定价演化：Every business needs to go through two pricing revolutions — move to usage-based, then to outcome-based. For me, if I can skip token-based, skip usage-based, and just say "Hey Patrick, what if I charge you for every good investment idea I give you?" or "what if I charge you for every SIM that you create as a banker?" — I'd much rather get there.

十五、路线图的 1%：资本市场的未来

Gabe：We are 1% of the way into our product roadmap. 99% of the innovation for capital markets is in front of us.

Think about the percentage of all capital markets workflows, investment workflows, investment banking jobs that are still completely human rate-limited.

类比 15-20 年前的房贷：every mortgage that someone got, you went in, you spoke to a banker at a local branch. No one ever thought you wouldn't want a human in the loop. Now, 40-50% of mortgages are just delivered online by platforms like Rocket Mortgage.

预测： - It'll be easier than ever for a business owner to go online and click a button to try to raise capital, the way someone can go on Robinhood and click a button to buy an equity. - It'll take 5 minutes for KKR to figure out "can I sell this portfolio company to another sponsor" — not 5 months. - You're going to be able to price assets in an order of magnitude less time. Markets are going to be more transparent, more liquid, more efficient.

十六、Bloomberg 策略：先数据，再工作流，最后交易所

Patrick：What do you need to build that you don't already have to enable that future?

Gabe：It's actually a very similar strategy to Bloomberg's: 1. Offer a little bit of data to get in the door 2. Build all the analytics and workflows on top 3. Provide the exchange and communication platform where you can transact across asset classes that before were pretty opaque (Bloomberg Messenger)

For us: 1. Use a little bit of AI to get in the door 2. Build out the full workflows — go from copilot chatbot to a full autopilot tool 3. Provide the communication channel between counterparties

But the difference is: I don't need to build the communication channel for humans to transact. I need to build the communication channel for the agents to transact.

Think about what system would allow a large private equity firm to feel comfortable having an agent negotiate a deal on its behalf, correspond with all third-party consultants (QoV, legal advisers), and run an auction process with sponsors providing bids. Huge amount of software to be built out.

We sometimes talk about it as an exchange for a lot of these asset classes that are not standardized.

十七、客户画像：为什么先攻大投行？

Gabe：Mostly large banks — very simply because that was my background. I worked as an investment banker for a handful of years doing buy-side M&A coverage.

Reasons to target banks: 1. Investment banks are the distribution channel for the rest of finance. A lot of great investors started as an analyst at Goldman in a TMT program. 2. They have the most seats by far. Landing Bank of America gets you into far more hands than landing 10 best single-PM public equities investors who each only have 10 investors.

十八、"个人生产力 → 公司生产力"的鸿沟

Patrick：How deep into the adoption curve are we for enterprises using AI?

Gabe：The majority of firms are seeing a huge amount of individual productivity and trying to figure out how to parlay that into firm productivity they can measure.

Speak to any individual banker: "I'm 100 times more efficient than I used to be." An MD says "I sent five pages to a client that before would have taken 3 days of back-and-forth with an analyst — I made it in 10 minutes myself." And these are bankers who haven't opened an Excel file in 20 years.

The problem: where's that flowing through? Are you winning more deals? Transacting more? Servicing a part of the market you haven't seen? It becomes a firm strategy problem.

Look at JP Morgan announcing they'll do a lot more M&A for SMBs — parts of the market that before didn't make sense to serve because deal fees were too small. Now if a banker can be a deal team of one, maybe you can enter parts of the market that made no sense before.

Patrick：So the bottleneck at some point will be the creativity of the customer.

Gabe：It's them figuring out what they want to do. If you had 100 great investors start here tomorrow working for you, how would you channel that productivity? What's the structure? How much money do I give each of them? What do we attack?

十九、准确性 vs. 可审计性

Patrick：Two years ago the most obvious question would have been about accuracy and "hallucinations" — I can't remember the last time someone said hallucinations to me.

Gabe：It's actually more important to be auditable than to be accurate. Obviously conflated — but what's important is: I give you an answer, you know how to use it. If it's not accurate and hard to see where it came from, you can't use it at all because you don't trust it. If it's accurate most of the time and even when it's not, it's very easy to see the assumptions and where the data was pulled from — it's still actionable.

Increasingly as these go from copilot (information retrieval) to autopilot (making an investment decision, sending an email), you need full confidence that if you went back to see why it made a decision, you'd understand why — because you're going to need to debug it.

Same way individual investors make horrible decisions and you go in to see what went wrong. Especially in capital markets with regulators — if you can't explain why you made a decision and the data that went in, that's not going to fly.

二十、如何以五倍速度招人？

Gabe：The core problem: how fast can you make a human being productive — as a salesperson, marketer, SDR, post-sales. Enablement and training and constantly retraining people is the fundamental problem.

Our internal tools are kind of magical: - Every internal conversation at Rogo is recorded 100%. "Hey, just FYI, Patrick, that's how we do." Not a Big Brother situation — everyone has Granola or some meeting transcription running because they need excellent recall. - We have a huge reservoir of information, and tools to pull it out contextually.

"Shrek" —— 公司大脑 It's called Shrek because my engineers thought it would be hilarious. There's a dashboard where you can see the swamp of everything people are working on. Connected to all our systems. Very prescriptive about company goals, values, north star metrics.

It's both proactive and reactive: - Someone can go in: "I'm trying to get up to speed on model routing and value prop for a large institution." - Or it can say: "Hey Patrick, I see on your calendar Thursday you're meeting with this private credit firm — here's all the information, all the use cases that will resonate, and all the ROI metrics that firms we've worked with would want to hear."

二十一、招聘 pitch：AI × 金融 = 人类进步

Gabe：AI is going to completely transform the world. The place that's going to be the most interesting is applied AI — because that's where AI intersects with humanity.

Finance is a domain that is the catalyst for all human progress and innovation. Capital allocation is upstream of the financing of every company, every idea, every economy. If you can make that more efficient, you can supercharge the world.

We're the category-leading player with the best shot on goal to not just be a $100 billion business, but the $500 billion business that completely transforms capital markets.

二十二、资本市场：为什么"减少摩擦"能改变世界

Patrick：Historically as markets get more efficient and liquid, their positive impact grows a lot.

Gabe：Look — you're always at risk of sounding like the billionaire private equity guy saying private equity is good for the world. But think about the origins of high finance.

JP Morgan 的起源：JP Pierpont Morgan helping connect European investors with the entrepreneurs in an emerging market (the United States) to finance railroads and the infrastructure buildout — everything that allowed the US to be a juggernaut economy. Intermediaries who helped connect capital allocators with entrepreneurs. That had a profoundly great effect on the world.

Now think about: - Every emerging nation where you'd struggle to raise capital, finance an idea, raise debt. - The 300,000 American businesses that couldn't even tell you what Goldman Sachs does, and JP Morgan doesn't have time to work with them because they're too small.

If you speed up the rate at which entrepreneurs and founders and individuals can tap into capital markets, you can accelerate all innovation.

[广告：Vanta、Ridgeline]

二十三、"嚼玻璃"：从同行创业者身上学到的

Gabe：I'm learning how much aggression it takes to grow this quickly. How much chewing glass it is on a day-to-day basis. How much conviction you need in the long-term TAM and SAM.

I'll call someone like Winston at Harvey. Winston's ability to just not worry about the hundred flesh wounds inflicted on him at any given time and just think about the end-state goal 3 years from now — that's pretty amazing.

"Chewing glass" 具体是什么？ - I worked during COVID — didn't even get to see what an office looked like. - John (co-founder) and I used to joke this is a very expensive business school education because we were doing everything wrong. Didn't know how to hire, fire, mentor, manage, give feedback, set direction. - When people quit, retention issues, spending 6 months recruiting a candidate who doesn't join — that's chewing glass. - Spending time on a product that gets completely washed over by the next model — chewing glass. - Getting rejected by 40 investors in a row — chewing glass.

Startup building is like a roller coaster with extreme highs and lows. I'm super emotional. But looking back 3 months at the low I was dealing with, I think "what a joke, I could do that in my sleep now."

二十四、Patrick Grady 的"两句话逻辑"

Gabe：Patrick Grady was at our board meeting on Wednesday. We presented an extremely aggressive plan for next year — hiring goals, commercial goals, product goals.

One of the reasons I love Pat is he boils everything down into two bullet points: "Premise one, premise two, this is the result." He went:

"Gabe, if everyone in finance is going to make a buying decision on AI in the next 18 months, and they are definitely going to buy something no matter what, even if you're not there — then the only thing that matters is that you can blitz the market as quickly as possible. Given that, do you think your plan is aggressive enough?"

The answer was no. Because I was being soft. You need to be so aggressive and underwrite all that risk. My goal as a venture-backed business is to increase the tails of the distribution. It's fine if the odds of failing rise 30% if the odds of becoming a $100 billion company also rise 20%.

二十五、Series A：被 40 家投资人拒绝

Gabe：When we were raising our Series A, we didn't have any star investors in our cap table yet. David Tisch at Box Group (an early pre-seed investor) introduced me to a bunch of all-time greats.

David introduced us to 40 investors. I met with everybody — Sequoia, Kleiner, Benchmark, everybody. 40 people passed.

And it wasn't like "oh, you get the email with the deck and it's not exciting." It was: - "Oh this is interesting, let me meet Gabe." - "I kind of like Gabe, let me spend an hour with him." - "Gabe, come to IC." - "Gabe, let's go to dinner." - "Gabe, come in for the weekend afterwards." - "You know what? We're going to pass."

It's so personal — at that stage it has nothing to do with anything but you. Like being broken up with by 40 girlfriends where every time you fell in love and every time they said "ah, not for you."

Thrive also passed at the Series A. Went to dinner with Avery and Vince, fell in love with them and the firm. Crushing blow.

Luckily Keith Rabois came about a month after everyone else rejected us. Keith said: "Gabe, this isn't a contrarian bet — it's basically just Harvey for finance. Why would I do it?" And I said: "Keith, if it's not contrarian, why did every single one of your friends just say it was a bad idea and not believe in me?"

Why didn't they believe? 1. People underappreciated the TAM in finance. Partly because SF has less intuition for finance — they didn't fund ION Group, Bloomberg, S&P, FactSet, Pitchbook, Morningstar. So no intuition for the contours of the market. 2. The product was terrible. Every investor said "oh, I work in finance, let me use it" — tried it, wrong half the time, "this is never going to work." I said "guys, we're on the exponential — it's going to work in 6 or 12 or 18 months." 3. People didn't think I could figure it out. They didn't have enough data points of watching me chew glass and figure out the next iteration.

二十六、为什么没有更多信誉的金融 AI 竞争者？

Gabe：Distribution is really hard to crack. It's far more a people problem — building trust, delivering value, working with these institutions — than just an engineering and product problem. But there's also an enormously high engineering and product burden.

I was so lucky that a number of the early people I hired were ex-finance and just killers. Hired folks from our network who worked at Goldman, Citi, Jefferies, Apollo, Ares, Blackstone. A team of people who were diehard, ambitious, curious, smart — and just good humans, low ego, humble, young enough to be open-minded.

二十七、技术人才的形态在变化

Patrick：How has your engineering and technical team looked over time?

Gabe：There are problems where domain expertise is increasing in value and having a GM-like mindset versus an engineer-like mindset is super important. There are also parts of our product where you just need raw gritty engineering talent because you're scaling aggressively.

A lot of the folks who have been excellent are former founders — people who started businesses, persevered, ate glass, had a lot of product intuition. The business may have petered out. We've acquired six different fledgling financial AI startups. Those former founders who can be galaxy-brained about the future while having engineering chops are super important.

二十八、创新者困境：金融业的第一次

Patrick：You said this is the first time we have a major innovator's dilemma in this category.

Gabe：For a lot of investment firms and high finance, the last 10-20 years have been pretty good. You can make a lot of money being a capital allocator. It's a very hard industry to enter — especially private markets, where when you raise a fund and another fund, it's hard to mess up the business.

But there hasn't been a moment and a shock to the market where every investment firm, every bank is saying: "Oh wow, I need to completely rethink what I'm doing. There's going to be an opportunity for hundreds of AI-native disruptors, AI-native investment firms, AI-native investment banks to attack my business model. What am I going to do?"

There has not been an innovator's dilemma for private equity firms, hedge funds, investment banks in a long time.

"AI native" 的定义：Willing to constantly reinvent everything you're doing. So AI-pilled that you don't worry about what seems far-fetched — you're charting a trajectory towards integrating this alien fundamental technology into everything. No part of the business you hold sacred that is immune to being revolutionized.

二十九、内部管理：AI 使用率的"红鼻子小丑帽"

Patrick：How do you as a leader make sure your company keeps doing this?

Gabe：A very simple thing: on a monthly basis I have a report showing everyone at the company how much they're using the various AI tools we have — both procured and built internally.

I have a stack ranking within every division of the top 5 power users and the bottom 5 users. We post it everywhere. And the bottom user in each division gets a printout with a dunce cap posted around the office.

It's hilarious but people know it's coming. As we get bigger and fewer people know me and know I'm kind of joking and funny — they're actually terrified. I hope that changes. But it's a strong incentive function.

三十、给传统投行/PE 老板的两个问题

Gabe： 1. If you knew for sure that right now 90% of your enterprise value is in your people — best investors, best bankers bringing in deals and revenue — and in 10 years the world's best investment firms/banks will have 90% of enterprise value not in people but in software, data, and systems — what would you start doing? You'd figure out how to take all of what lives in the latent minds of your best people and put it into a system you own and operate autonomously.

  1. Unpack every part of the deal lifecycle. In each one, chart where you think you are invaluable — you have data, domain expertise, or relationships no one else has. Then be diligent: do I actually have something no one else has, or do I just think I'm smarter and better-read? Because if it's the latter, AI is going to obviate that.

三十一、预见未来的典范：Moelis 的 Ken Moelis

Patrick：Have you seen anyone be the most cutting-edge exemplar?

Gabe：The folks that today look the most prescient sounded batshit two years ago. Two years ago people were like "what the heck is Patrick talking about?"

One example: Ken Moelis, founder of Moelis. He was prescient about where it was going. He wanted: - Digital clones of all their best bankers - Systems that could show up to calls, speak on his behalf, know how he thinks - Any junior at the investment bank could leverage his expertise, context, and relationships immediately

So context and data wasn't just powering his ability to be revenue-generating — it was empowering every junior in the bank. His "Move 37" moment.

三十二、最大的不确定性：人类的"握手依恋"

Patrick：What feels the most uncertain about the future of your business?

Gabe： 1. How quickly private markets actually transform. Asset classes increase in liquidity through standardization because it gets easier to track and trade them. Private markets have been immune to standardization because there's so much unstructured data — AI should fix that. But will there be a regulatory or market force that forces additional standardization? That's out of my control.

  1. How much alpha will be left in human relationships? Take micro-cap M&A: if you're a small business owner who built a business for 20 years, wanting to make sure you can trust whoever you hand it to — it's very hard to imagine that being fully automated.

But for a lot of sponsor-owned businesses, secondaries, private credit, GP-LP secondaries — I think it can be fully automated. How long it takes for the long tail of small and medium businesses dealing with generational turnover to get comfortable clicking a button instead of shaking a hand — that's up in the air.

三十三、给创业者：如何和 VC 打交道

Gabe：My style for fundraising might not be everyone's: - Super direct. Super transparent about what I'm worried about and where I want to go. - Be very headstrong on that end state. - It's about reps and relationships. The folks who come out of nowhere and lead the Series C or D are the folks I met at the seed, then A, then B, then C — and they passed every time for all sorts of reasons, but gathered a lot more data on me.

What not to do：A lot of the "fake it till you make it." You need bravado and confidence in what you're doing even if you're not fully confident. I'm a deeply paranoid, deeply insecure, deeply scared person. But you need to put on the face.

People misinterpret that as pretending to be something they're not. That's not true. You need to believe that 5% likelihood of being a $100 billion business is likely — and delineate with a very clear roadmap and strategy how it's possible.

三十四、为什么害怕？为什么不安全？

Patrick：Why are you scared and insecure?

Gabe：I'm so paranoid about everything that can go wrong. Every day feels like you're on the knife's edge of a thousand things collapsing.

Startup building is a game of compounding momentum. How do you do every small thing to race a little faster downhill? I'm scared the momentum will stop — you hit a roadblock, go off course, need to reinitialize momentum.

It's so clear how hard it is to build a machine that gathers momentum. If I wasn't constantly petrified of those moments, I wouldn't be doing everything under the sun to prepare for them.

三十五、被遗漏的：黑洞效应

Patrick：What have we missed?

Gabe：There are going to be businesses that solve all these problems. But the businesses that do will become black holes for talent, capital, and brand. They'll siphon in resources to actually execute.

AI is an amazing tailwind, but the execution bar is higher than ever. Everyone is getting pulled into the big leagues, having their "welcome to the NFL" moment. You have to move faster, be stronger, more resilient and agile than you ever expected.

Having the right team is more important than ever. And the right team is extremely expensive. If you can't figure out the strategy to become a black hole for talent and capital as quickly as possible, you are far more at risk of being roadkill of a lab or a company that can.

三十六、最后一个问题：最善意的事

Patrick：What is the kindest thing anyone's ever done for you?

Gabe：I benefited so much from having parents who were enormously kind, generous, selfless — but it showed up in different ways.

My mother：No matter what I did, I was amazing and smart and could do no wrong. Even though growing up that was absolutely not the case. But she instilled in me the confidence to believe in myself. Even in low trajectories — 40 no's in a row, flunking out, failing — she acted like I was maybe the smartest person on earth. It was irrational, but you need some of that irrational confidence that comes from undying love.

My father：Very different. If I came home having done something wrong, he'd be seething, could barely look at me. He was so disciplined, had such high standards. His version of kindness was figuring out who I am and why I am failing at this thing, and then helping me. He'd sit down and go over every detail with me — even though he sometimes couldn't understand why I couldn't take advantage of the opportunities I had — and take time to make me better while staying true to his principles and definitions of excellence.

Patrick：You're building a fascinating business. It's been so cool to watch it get better. Thanks for doing this with me.

Gabe：Thank you.

[结束广告：Ramp、Vanta、WorkOS、Ridgeline]

item.description:
## 隐藏的系统性洞察
**意外观察：这不是一个 AI 公司的故事，而是一个"人类知识液态化"的故事**
大多数人听 Gabe 的访谈，会把 Rogo 理解为"金融领域的 Harvey"或"投行的 ChatGPT"。但真正的隐藏叙事在他不经意的一句话里：**"你要开始把最优秀的人脑中那些潜在的东西，装进你自己拥有和运营的系统里。"** 这句话的颠覆性在于——他描述的不是效率工具，而是一场**关于"人力资本所有权"的世纪级转移**。
过去 200 年，投行和对冲基金的核心资产是"关系"和"直觉"，这些资产**寄生在人脑里**，会跟着人跳槽而流失（想想 2008 年后美林向摩根士丹利的人才大迁徙）。Rogo 本质上是在提供一种**"知识产权固化技术"**——把明星银行家的隐性知识从"随时可能离职的碳基载体"中蒸馏出来，注入到"雇主拥有的硅基载体"中。这与其说是软件生意，不如说是**劳动关系史上的一次相变**。你会发现 Gabe 内部工具叫"Shrek"、强制记录所有对话、公开羞辱 AI 使用率最低的员工——这些不是管理风格，是**知识殖民的仪式化过程**。
## 跨领域连接：Rog
