item.description:
## 三个意外的系统性观察
### 1. Nike 的悖论：它不是"输给了政治正确"，而是"输给了自己解锁的信任门"
表面叙事说 Nike 是"go woke go broke"的典型。但真正的系统性真相埋得更深——**Nike 的崩塌是"直销革命"和"文化站队"两个独立决策在同一个时间点形成的死亡交叉**。
想想这个隐藏的机制：当 Nike 把消费者从 Foot Locker、JD Sports 的货架上拽到自己的 App 里时，它其实是在做一个惊人的信任赌注——"你必须已经决定要买 Nike，才会打开这个 App。" 这意味着 Nike 主动放弃了"被偶然发现"和"在竞品旁被选中"的权利。
而恰恰在这个时刻，它选择了 Kaepernick。这就形成了一个致命的系统耦合：**当品牌需要消费者"预先决定爱你"时，你却给了他们"预先讨厌你"的理由。** 传统零售渠道能吸收政治争议——因为消费者是在货架前做冲动决定的；但 DTC 渠道放大了品牌"信仰门槛"的成本。这是两个看起来独立的战略，在心理学层面形成了乘法效应的灾难。
### 2. 跨领域连接：Sydney Sweeney

item.title: [No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups] Why Diffusion Will Win AI Inference with Inception Co-Founder and CEO Stefano Ermon
item.dc:creator: No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个被忽视的历史反讽：Diffusion 正在扮演 2017 年 Transformer 的角色

最令人意外的洞察藏在 Stefano 随口提及的一个类比里，但他自己没有把这层含义完全展开：这场"自回归 vs 扩散"之争，本质上是 2017 年"RNN vs Transformer"之争的一次时空错位重演。

  • 2017 年：RNN 在训练时被"顺序性"卡住 → Transformer 用并行化解放训练
  • 2026 年：自回归模型在推理时被"顺序性"卡住 → Diffusion 用并行化解放推理

换句话说，整个 LLM 生态正走向一个几何对称的困境：我们用一种"训练时并行"的架构（Transformer）承载了一种"推理时串行"的生成范式（autoregressive）。这就像用高速公路运货，却规定每辆车必须等前一辆到达终点才能出发。Diffusion 不是"另一种架构"，而是补齐了 Transformer 革命尚未完成的另一半——把并行性从训练环节延伸到推理环节。谁先意识到这一层，谁就能理解为什么 Ermon 敢押注这条路。

跨领域连接：Diffusion 的"控制哲学"，和精益制造、司法程序惊人相似

Stefano 提到 diffusion 相对自回归模型的一个隐藏优势——可控性：你不必等生成完整对象再评分，而可以在"粗到细"的过程中不断纠偏。这个特性让我立刻联想到两个看似无关的领域：

  1. 丰田生产系统的"安东绳"（Andon Cord）：任何工人在任何环节都可以拉绳停线，而不是等成品下线才检验。自回归模型是"传统流水线"——必须成品才验货；diffusion 是"精益制造"——每一道工序都可介入。
  2. 英美普通法 vs 大陆法系：普通法是"边审边形成"（迭代精炼），大陆法是"依既定条文推导到结论"（前向生成）。Diffusion 的迭代去噪，更接近 common law 的思维方式。

这意味着 diffusion 模型未来很可能会开启一整类自回归模型根本无法提供的"过程干预型" API——想象一个法律 AI 允许你在推理过程中随时"注入约束"，或一个分子生成模型让化学家在每一步"投票"选择方向。这不是速度问题，而是人机协作范式的变化。

隐藏的真相：Inception 真正的护城河不是模型，而是"stack 不兼容"

表面上看 Inception 的卖点是速度，但 Stefano 反复强调一件事：他们不得不自己造推理引擎（vLLM/SGLang 不能用）、自己造 SFT/RLHF 栈、自己写 kernel。这听起来是劣势，但存在一个反直觉的战略含义：

在一个"大厂会吸收所有架构创新"的时代，护城河反而藏在"不能被吸收"的东西里——即那些必须重写才能启用新范式的底层基础设施。

大厂可以在一夜之间加一个 diffusion 训练目标，但他们不可能在一夜之间抛弃 vLLM、抛弃已优化的 kernel 库、抛弃两年积累的 RL 基础设施。这就是所谓的"架构切换成本"护城河——它和当年 Nvidia 的 CUDA 生态是同构的：真正卡住对手的不是算法，而是围绕算法长出的整个软件栈的路径依赖。

有意思的是，如果 Inception 全部开源，反而会削弱这个护城河（大厂会免费拿走整套 stack）。所以他们选择"半闭源"——这不是保守，而是对"生态位不对称"最精明的博弈选择。一个咨询式的追问是：Ermon 是否在潜意识里，在复刻 Nvidia 早年的策略？

📝 转录文本

Why Diffusion Will Win AI Inference — Stefano Ermon (Inception) 访谈

主持人（开场介绍）： Hi listeners, welcome back to No Priors. Today I'm here with Stephenau Man who is a longtime Stanford professor and now co-founder and CEO of Inception. Stephenau has a extraordinarily broad body of work around generative modeling, but is especially well known as one of the fathers of diffusion. We talk about his company challenging the large labs and why speed and efficiency are going to be the name of the game in AI over the next few years. Welcome Stepheno.

Stepheno, thanks so much for being here.

Stefano：Great to be here.

一、研究背景：从冷门方向到 Diffusion 的诞生

主持人：I would love for us to just start with a little bit of your research background and how you ended up starting your company.

Stefano：For sure. Yeah. I've been doing research in generative models for like uh basically my entire career. I started at Stanford in 2014 as an assistant professor and I was working on building generative models. Back then the research area was not particularly hot. The models were not quite working well. We were still like building little generative models over MNIST and it was like a big success if you could generate these grainy images of digits. It was even hard to publish papers back then on that topic, and you had to kind of like justify training a generative model as a way to learn features from unlabelled data that then could maybe help you do better at supervised learning — because that was the thing that everybody cared about.

But then things took over of course, and so I was at the right place at the right time working on the right thing. I've been doing research in that space since the beginning basically.

主持人：Did you have, besides a curiosity in the area, a personal hope for what the models would do back in 2014 and 15?

Stefano：Yeah. I always felt like that was the right way to think about learning from unlabelled data — that building a generative model is really the right way to make sure you understand the structure in the data. I was not even dreaming about the kind of capabilities that these LLMs that we have today could do. I was thinking more from a world models perspective. I was working a lot on images and thinking: okay, if I have a world model, I can imagine what's going to happen if I were to stand up and walk out the door. I can kind of picture that in my mind, and that's important to make decisions and kind of like model predictive control. Having this kind of model of the world requires some generative capabilities.

I always felt like that's the right direction to work on. I felt like this is going to be very hard as a problem, it's going to keep me busy for my whole career and it's a good problem to work on. And then of course I was very wrong and things evolved much faster than I was expecting.

二、从 Score-based 到 Diffusion：一次范式转折

主持人：Yeah, I think that's kind of universally true. Sort of walk me through the state of your research and how that led you to start the company.

Stefano：So I was working on generative models of images, initially working on autoregressive models which were very slow and kind of like very blurry, and then VAEs, and then GANs took over.

Back then we were very unhappy with the state of generative models for images — the GANs worked but they were very unstable to train, very hard to reproduce results. So we were trying to see: is there a way to build something that is as good as GANs but more principled?

We started working on score-based generative models which are basically what eventually became diffusion models — back in 2019 with my PhD student. We came up with this idea: let's train a neural network to denoise images. If you can denoise an image, then you really are understanding enough about the structure of the image that it should be possible to build a generative procedure based on these denoisers.

That basically became the underlying technology of modern diffusion models — where instead of generating images left to right one pixel at a time, you start from pure noise and then you gradually refine the object until you get a clean picture at the end.

That started back in 2019 in my lab and then it kind of took over the space. Even today the best models for image generation, video generation, music to some extent, a lot of the protein stuff — they are based on diffusion. My group has worked a lot on various kinds of diffusion models: techniques for accelerating them to generate samples very quickly, and to improve the quality of these models.

Since we were able to get them to work on images, I started thinking about how do we get diffusion models to work on text or code generation and discrete objects. Is there a way to move beyond autoregressive models to something that's more parallel, more built-in error correction? So I've been doing a bunch of research at Stanford on getting diffusion models to work on text and code generation.

We had a breakthrough in 2024. We published a paper basically showing that for the first time it was possible to match the quality of an autoregressive model at the GPT-2 scale — less than a billion parameters, still fairly academic. But we were able to train basically still a transformer model as a diffusion model on the same data, and match the quality (the same perplexity, fitting the data just as well as an autoregressive model with the same number of parameters). The diffusion model was significantly faster because it's diffusion — you're outputting many tokens at the same time. We were able to generate text like 10× faster compared to the autoregressive model.

That felt very very exciting. I really wanted to see what happens if you scale up, if you train bigger models. So I started Inception — a company to basically scale up the technology and try to build commercial-scale diffusion-based language models.

三、为什么 Diffusion 在推理时会赢

主持人：Everyone has now seen the outputs of diffusion models — in particular images. I would argue that increasingly, short-form video generated from diffusion models is a dominant form of entertainment in other parts of the world, and it will likely become so here. It's kind of unbelievable, at least to me even having followed the field for the last decade plus, the quality that is possible today.

That is kind of obvious, and it's such a big use case in images and video generation that folks are even creating hardware to support better performance here. But it's not intuitive that this would work for other fields, or that this is an interesting competitive direction to the current full-transformer-focused AGI labs. Can you offer some intuition on that?

Stefano：Yeah, so it's a very interesting kind of state of the world right now from a researcher perspective. There are two main paradigms — two ways of building generative models.

  • Autoregressive: you have a model that predicts the next token or the next pixel, and then you generate left to right one token at a time.
  • Diffusion: coarse-to-fine generation, iterative denoising.

As you said, we have continuous modalities where diffusion dominates. And there are discrete modalities — text and code — where primarily all the big labs are betting on the same architecture: autoregressive models.

As we move towards more multimodal models, and this idea that maybe we'll have a model that can handle all modalities and will know everything about the world — what architecture will that be? Will it be an autoregressive model or a diffusion model? Nobody knows. The jury is still out there.

At Inception we're betting on diffusion models because we believe that what matters eventually will be inference-time scaling, and there are fundamental reasons for why diffusion models are better than autoregressive models at inference time.

一个关键的历史类比

Even if you think about the story of autoregressive models — there was an inflection point in 2017 when people switched from RNNs to transformers, right? Why? The problem was that RNNs had to essentially process tokens sequentially, one at a time, and training was very slow. So people came up with this idea: let's have an architecture that allows you to process many tokens at the same time in parallel. That was the transformer, and that was the thing that scaled better for training and enabled a lot of the successes behind LLMs.

But if you think about inference now — not training, inference/generation — autoregressive models are still sequential. The computation is left-to-right, one token at a time. You cannot generate the 10th token until you've generated everything that comes before it. That kind of workload does not map well to GPUs. That kind of workload is extremely memory-bound. You're spending most of your time moving around weights across the memory hierarchy and you're doing very little arithmetic. That's a fundamental problem of autoregressive models.

So what's the equivalent? If you think RNN → transformers (for training), the equivalent at inference time is a diffusion model — because a diffusion model is built to have, at inference time, a workload where you process many tokens at the same time. The workload at inference time in a diffusion model is basically very very similar to the workload you have for training, where you're processing many tokens at the same time in parallel.

It's built to essentially have an inference workload that maps really well to matmuls — the kind of things GPUs do really well.

经济性驱动一切

We bet on trying to build the architecture and the kind of models that will scale best at inference time — because economics are dominated by the kind of intelligence per watt, the intelligence per dollar that you're able to get from the models.

If you think about a lot of the advances with reasoning models, a lot of it is scaling test-time compute. Being able to scale better along that axis will also matter.

Even if you think about RL post-training, a lot of the bottleneck is generating rollouts — letting the model explore, scoring the trajectories, and then improving the model based on the kind of things it finds. Inference is again a key bottleneck for RL post-training. So if you have a model that scales better at inference time, then automatically you're going to get better scaling during RL post-training.

That's why we decided to bet on a diffusion-based LLM: because it's inherently more parallel — and the bitter lesson is that the more parallel solution is the one that is eventually going to win.

四、离散 vs 连续：破解 Text/Code 上的难题

主持人：How did you think about applicability — or what experiments did you run — in terms of cracking the nut on discrete versus continuous modalities? People have also shaped the existing dominant paradigm through new tokenization efforts or methods to make video and voice work, for example. You're not in the same token-oriented paradigm. How do you make it work here?

Stefano：Yeah, there was a lot of research that went into figuring out how to apply a technology that was inherently very tied to continuous structure in the data.

If you think about a diffusion model, it's learning how to denoise images, and it makes sense for continuous data because if you think about two pixel colors, you can kind of interpolate between them and it will still make sense. But if you think about two words, there is not necessarily something in between them, right? It's all discrete. It required a lot of R&D and a new science that had to be developed to figure out how to extend those ideas to discrete spaces.

主持人：What can you claim about how well it works today?

Stefano：We think it works really well. We've been able to train diffusion-based LLMs that are comparable in quality with the speed-optimized models from Frontier Labs. Our Mercury models are on par with the Haiku models, Flash models, Mini/Nano models from OpenAI if you look at benchmarks — while being significantly faster.

We've gone from pure research prototypes to things that are actually used. We are serving these models in production today. We did all the work of figuring out how to even just build a serving engine — you cannot run these diffusion-based LLMs on vLLM or SGLang, we had to build our own serving engine. We can handle a lot of the complexity of real production workloads, and we've solved all these challenges. We can deliver this kind of new experience end-to-end to real customers today.

五、公司现状与差异化

主持人：Actually a great time to just talk about where Inception is as a company — how many people, what are you guys actually serving, sort of state of research?

Stefano：We are about two years old, around 50 people. Spending a lot of time still on R&D — figuring out what's the right way to train these models, how to accelerate inference.

It's not obvious. Even if you think about an autoregressive model it's pretty clear: you generate one token at a time and that's it. In a diffusion-based model, we know that there is a lot of different possibilities for trading compute for quality at inference time. Even if you think about image or video diffusion models, there's a lot of techniques you can use to accelerate sampling — distillation, or fancy differential equation solving techniques that allow you to sample very quickly from these models.

There is a lot of research on training, on inference, and then engineering — thinking about data mixes, evals, RL post-training infrastructure. There is a lot of work that needs to happen to figure out how to build recipes that work for this new model.

We try to leverage existing things as much as possible. For example, it's still a transformer-based model — you don't have to throw away a lot of the work that has been done on good architectures. We still use attention, we still use a lot of the public datasets that people have created, and evals and benchmarks. We're a startup, we try to be scrappy, we try to use existing things as much as possible, and focus on the aspects where we can have the highest impact and where we can be the most differentiated.

Right now it's speed. In the future, who knows? It's possible that a diffusion-based language model will be significantly more intelligent than an autoregressive one — nobody knows. That's why I think this is very exciting: we're developing these really powerful AI systems but it's all very fresh, all very new. I doubt we've discovered the best way of building these systems. There's got to be alternatives, other ways of building these models. Eventually, efficiency will be very important.

If you think about the AI factory — how is that going to work? I think nobody really knows. Just being able to play in that space and thinking about alternative ways of creating intelligence — I think it's exciting.

六、Speed 已在哪里赢下市场：语音代理案例

主持人：Absolutely. In an increasingly fundamentally compute and supply constrained environment, focus on efficiency wasn't the primary consideration for many industrial research efforts versus pure capability scaling. But if you fundamentally believe that we can use all of the power we have, and there will be economic reasons to do so, then the focus on efficiency is going to go dramatically up.

One of the most important decisions for a company in the AI space is how do we use the power we have between training and the most valuable use cases for any watt. On that topic — here in September of '26 — where does speed win, where do people care enough about this already?

Stefano：It is basically applications where latency matters. Generally speaking, everyone cares about speed in the sense that if you can give me the same quality but faster, people will always pick the faster solution. We're seeing it with faster versions of even the models from Frontier Labs — people are willing to pay more to get access to faster models.

Once you get used to a fast model, it's hard to go back. It's kind of like broadband — you get faster and faster, and once you get the fast model, people cannot go back.

主持人：Are there customers that you can talk about publicly that care about this today?

Stefano：There are a few that we can mention. In the voice space for example — OpenCall is an example. They're building voice agents. Speed of course — the pipeline is: you have an ASR model, you have an LLM doing tool calls and figuring out what to say next (it has to be a reasoning LLM typically to have the highest level of quality), and then there is a text-to-speech component at the end. Speed matters a lot.

They were previously using — serving their LLMs on Cerebras. They were using custom chips to get to the kind of speed they need to deliver the best experience to their customers. Then they switched over to our diffusion-based LLMs because they can essentially get the same speed as what you would get if you were to run an autoregressive model on custom hardware.

If you have a diffusion-based LLM that's built to be parallel, accelerated at the software level, then you can get the same speed on Nvidia GPUs — which means much more availability. GPUs are scarce, but there's more of that than custom chips. Lower cost, higher quality. That's an example in the voice space.

主持人：I was actually going to ask you how you think this interacts with the hardware landscape as well, given we've seen enough demand from use cases who are like — yes, I want a big expensive chip with a lot of SRAM and people will pay for the outputs of that — in coding and other use cases.

Stefano：For sure. Hardware is one way to accelerate things — and the good thing…

主持人：…and software might be better if we can use the existing hardware.

Stefano：Exactly. And especially they are complementary. That's the exciting piece — the gains you get from software are multiplicative with the gains you get from hardware. Maybe someday people will develop hardware that fits even better the models we're building. For sure.

七、面对大厂 David vs Goliath 的护城河

主持人：If we zoom out to Inception in the broader industry — I think there is a vein of concern, and correct me if I'm wrong, that it's very hard to invest in new architectures today, because if there are advances in architecture or methods, it will simply be absorbed by large players with the resources to scale compute. Talk to me about how you think about going and competing as David in this situation.

Stefano：It's a very valid point and something that is also top of mind for us.

Initially for us, the moat is sort of the IP, the trade secrets, the ideas that we and our researchers have to build these models and make them better. As we mature as a company — and one of the reasons we are not just doing pure research but we've also developed a product, have real customers, and are getting feedback on the models from the real world — is that by doing that we are also developing components that are very important to deploy these models.

For example — a serving engine. If you don't have the serving engine, you can't really serve these models in production. By forcing ourselves from the very beginning to go out and deploy something end-to-end, we're learning a lot about how to serve these models and how to build software that's needed to run these models. That again becomes IP. Even if you train the diffusion-based LLM, if you don't have the serving engine, if you don't have the vLLM equivalent to serve it, you're still stuck.

Along the same lines: we are working with real customers and getting feedback on the models. We figure out what works, what doesn't. We collect data sometimes from them. We create evals based on what they're seeing. That again becomes part of the technical moat, because those things are a little bit harder to replicate.

八、Code/Text 数据的"噪声"问题：Diffusion 也 OK 吗？

主持人：You can tell me if this doesn't make sense as a question to ask technically — but one of the things that diffusion models benefit from structurally in images or video generation is you're replicating something where there should be some consistent structure in the world. Voice as well. It is whatever is really possible and most likely.

Some of the fields where AI has been most valuable to date — a lot of the input data you use to train, like code data — it's very messy, right? One could argue that a lot of it doesn't actually have the correct real structure you're looking for. How do you think about that when it's human-generated input data versus images, video, voice?

Stefano：It's a good question. Fundamentally, if you think about whenever you train a generative model — whether it's an autoregressive model or to some extent even a diffusion model — you are trying to identify structure in the data by essentially building a compression scheme. That might not be obvious, but whenever you train these models, you're effectively trying to identify common structure by trying to find an efficient way of compressing the data.

The more you can compress the data, the more structure, the more patterns you're identifying. And that's how these models work — which is the amazing thing: just by predicting the next word, you are learning something about the structure of the data. That's the same whether you're using a diffusion model or an autoregressive model. Both methods are essentially trying to learn a compression scheme.

When I mentioned the original 2024 paper — where we showed we are achieving parity with autoregressive models — the metric we're using is basically perplexity, which is a notion of how much structure have you identified in the data. Even though it might not seem obvious, we were actually able to identify at the GPT-2 scale the same amount of structure as an autoregressive model.

主持人：I think that empirical result is there, but the intuition would be — well, code is not the dataset grounded in physics, there's a lot of noise in there. It sounds like you believe that's a manageable problem.

Stefano：There is noise in everything. To the extent — the numbers don't lie — that you're able to drive the perplexity down, then it means that you can actually build a compression scheme that will get you that level of compression. So the structure must be there, and the model must have been able to uncover it.

Then it's more a question of an inductive bias — is a transformer a better way of identifying those patterns, or something else? Is next-token prediction the right modeling framework, or is it more like denoising? That's very much an empirical question that at the moment we don't have the tools even to understand.

九、可控性：一个被低估的优势

主持人：Can I ask a question — since you used a voice customer as the example here — one of the benefits that some people building these AI products have identified of having an LLM in the middle of this voice pipeline is they understand how to do alignment a little bit better there, or controllability. I imagine that has to look different for a diffusion-based model. Can you talk about that?

Stefano：Yes, that's a key value proposition. One of the things they always look into is: to what extent — a lot of the value they provide is like the harness and making sure that the models indeed are doing the right thing.

The interesting thing about a diffusion-based LLM is that we've built everything to be backwards compatible. The API is the same — still OpenAI-compatible, text in, text out. The models we've trained are good at following instructions, good at outputting structured outputs (JSONs, etc.). They can handle all of those things.

It was good enough — in fact better than the models they were using before. So they are still able to provide the level of service to their customers by using Mercury.

Very simply, if the interfaces are the same, you can just use your same stack.

But — and this is actually a very interesting point — we know that diffusion models are typically easier to control compared to autoregressive models. The reason is: if you think about an autoregressive model, you have to wait until you've generated the full object to know whether or not it satisfies, say, a constraint, or whether it's aligned, or whether it matches your objective function. Maybe you're generating a molecule and you care about solubility — you have to wait until you have the full object to be able to score it with some reward function.

But a diffusion model is coarse-to-fine generation. From the very beginning you know kind of like — is this object the kind of thing I want or not? — and you can steer the generation in the direction provided by an external reward function or some set of constraints.

There is a lot of evidence in the academic literature at least that diffusion models are easier to control, and there are different ways of steering them that are just not possible with autoregressive models. So that would be a different interface for the model that might not even be available for autoregressive models. That's something we've been thinking a lot about — what's the right product experience we can build around new capabilities that are just not provided by autoregressive models.

十、涌现能力与数据效率

主持人：Are there capabilities that you imagine in Inception's models having at scale that today's models don't have beyond performance?

Stefano：Yeah, that's the thing — we don't know. It's emergent. Right now the wedge is speed — we know they are much faster. That was the initial bet because that was easier to test, easy to measure, and obviously valuable. But that's why I find it so exciting: as we learn more about how to train these models, we don't know what we're going to find.

There is a decent amount of evidence in the academic literature that diffusion-based models are more data-efficient compared to autoregressive models. The intuition is: if you think about training a diffusion model, you're learning by denoising. You start with an image, you add noise, and then you learn how to remove the noise. It's effectively doing data augmentation in the sense that the same image is augmented by many noisy views.

They tend to be a little bit more data-efficient. So if that holds up at scale, then maybe we'll get into tasks where we have less data — where data becomes the bottleneck. Then it becomes more interesting.

That's why it's so exciting — things are changing, and this technology is so important and so valuable that having something differentiated will create value.

十一、两年后的工作负载分布

主持人：If we project out five years — that's actually way too long in AI world — if we project out two years, what do you think is the workload split between diffusion and traditional models?

Stefano：We're not at the frontier level of intelligence, and a lot of the workloads do require frontier-level intelligence. But in my estimates — even if you just go to OpenRouter, they have a very nice way of looking at all the different use cases: research, conversational, coding, software engineering, log processing… they have a nice hard taxonomy of tasks.

I was doing some estimates, and I think there is like between 20 and 30% where latency is really important. So at the very least as a lower bound, I think it could be addressable by models that — within a given latency budget — will give you the highest possible quality.

十二、Diffusion 的挑战：整个 stack 都得自己造

主持人：All technology approaches have trade-offs — what are the challenges of working with diffusion models?

Stefano：It's a different stack, so one of the challenges is we had to build a lot of things in-house. There is not a mature ecosystem — if you think about the serving engine or kernels — a lot of the things had to be developed in-house.

There is not really anything open-source. There are some open-source models but they're not particularly good. So that makes it a little bit more difficult to deploy, to get customers to try things — they're not used to it.

主持人：I imagine that also reflects externally — in a landscape where folks at some sophistication would care about cost and performance from the beginning, there's an increasing amount of interest in post-training. So I imagine in a new architecture that's even more challenging.

Stefano：We had to build our own stack for doing SFT, for doing RLHF, doing RL. I mean, that becomes IP to some extent. It's one of the reasons we decided not to open-source everything — really to keep the IP a little bit closer to us and not opening it up. But then there are downsides: less opportunity for the community to contribute, harder to adopt, hard to do on-prem deployments. There are pros and cons with the two choices.

十三、团队与人才吸引

主持人：Can you talk about scale of your own training — current or aspirational — and at 50 people I'm sure you're continuing to hire. Why should researchers or engineers consider investing in this direction or working here?

Stefano：We're not able to share much about the training, the size of the models, or the flops — it's kind of a trade secret. But we are continuing to push the frontier.

Inception is a great place to be if you want to have an opportunity to shape the direction of the field. It's still a relatively small field. There is a lot to be invented. A lot of the people that decide to come to Inception instead of joining one of the other labs — they really want to have ownership. They like to invent new things. They like to be in a space where there's more of a green field and more opportunities to try things. There's less that's known or available out there. It's a little bit more open-ended, and so we tend to attract those kinds of people.

十四、递归自我改进与人类创造力

主持人：I think one thing that is both exciting and causes some despair amongst research friends is the ability to use models for recursive self-improvement in the research field itself. Given you're working on a very different direction, what is your view on this?

Stefano：I mean, it's something that we —

主持人：Implicitly, it sounds like you still feel there's work for you and your team to do.

Stefano：Oh yeah. We're not there yet. Maybe we don't have access to the models that other folks have, but I feel like — we use models a lot of course, and it has accelerated the speed at which we can iterate, try ideas. We use models from Frontier Labs and it's been great. It has accelerated our development process a lot.

At the same time, right now — I don't know what it's going to be in six months or a year — but right now, human ingenuity is still super important. The ability to come up with the right ideas and prune the space and identify directions that are more promising has been really important to us.

50 people is not that many people for a full-stack research/serving/product company. How do you organize and how do you think about how you allocate your resources here?

Stefano：It's a small team but everyone is very talented and they work very hard, and we have access to agents that are making us a lot more productive. So I think the numbers are sufficient to do a lot. In fact, often the bottleneck is more compute than people.

The team is organized like: there is a product team that is handling the platform and working with customers to make them successful with our models. Then there is a team that is serving the current best version of the model. And there is a team that is building the next version of the model — that includes training, RL, inference. So that's more research.

十五、学术界的价值：Contrarian Bets

主持人：Stefano, one last question for you. The '24 paper was a super interesting result, made a big splash. You've been working in this field for a long time. A lot of folks would claim that academic AI research is very challenged in this era of being able to scale resource a great deal. This is certainly true to some degree given you started a commercial company around it as well. But how did you get confidence in the directions that you were working in having impact or being promising before you really had those '24 results?

Stefano：It was a collection of results that I had been working on in my lab. Of course, there's the early diffusion work — we showed that at the kind of scale of models we could train academically, we were able to beat GANs, while being much more stable. And then the whole thing took over and became Stable Diffusion, Midjourney — all of that started from ideas developed in academia, in my lab.

But that's not the only one. I was co-advisor — I worked on FlashAttention, for example. That's another thing that came out of academia and eventually had a huge impact in industry.

Another example is DPO — that was another project that started out as a rotation project in my group. It's an algorithm used to align LLMs and diffusion models everywhere. That was developed entirely in academia — based on a clever insight, some interesting mathematical structure in that problem that allows you to come up with a very different and more efficient way of post-training and aligning these models.

There are gems — lots of opportunities for finding new and better ways of solving important problems. One of the nice things about academia is that it allows you to take these contrarian bets. As you said, there is the challenge that maybe we don't have enough resources — and there's never enough resources; if we had more compute we could be more efficient. But you have access to amazing students, and everyone is trying to develop the new thing. People are not scared about taking bets. That's why academia has been so impactful — in the AI space, a lot of the important ideas have roots or were created in academia.

主持人：Awesome. Super inspirational. Thanks so much for being here, Stefano.

Stefano：Thank you so much for having me.

Find us on Twitter at @NoPriorsPod. Subscribe to our YouTube channel if you want to see our faces. Follow the show on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you listen — that way you get a new episode every week. And sign up for emails or find transcripts for every episode at no-priors.com.

item.description:
## 一个被忽视的历史反讽：Diffusion 正在扮演 2017 年 Transformer 的角色
最令人意外的洞察藏在 Stefano 随口提及的一个类比里，但他自己没有把这层含义完全展开：**这场"自回归 vs 扩散"之争，本质上是 2017 年"RNN vs Transformer"之争的一次时空错位重演**。
- 2017 年：RNN 在训练时被"顺序性"卡住 → Transformer 用并行化解放训练 - 2026 年：自回归模型在推理时被"顺序性"卡住 → Diffusion 用并行化解放推理
换句话说，整个 LLM 生态正走向一个几何对称的困境：我们用一种"训练时并行"的架构（Transformer）承载了一种"推理时串行"的生成范式（autoregressive）。这就像用高速公路运货，却规定每辆车必须等前一辆到达终点才能出发。**Diffusion 不是"另一种架构"，而是补齐了 Transformer 革命尚未完成的另一半**——把并行性从训练环节延伸到推理环节。谁先意识到这一层，谁就能理解为什么 Ermon 敢押注这条路。
## 跨领域连接：Diff

item.title: [Lex Clips] Deadly & horrible attempts by doctors to cure insanity | Andrew Scull and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、精神病学最致命的悖论：唯一真正的胜利，成为最惨烈失败的模板

这段对话中隐藏着一个令人毛骨悚然的结构性讽刺——精神病学史上极少数确凿的生物学发现（梅毒螺旋体导致 GPI），恰恰成了随后半个世纪灾难性医疗暴行的"授权文件"。当 20 世纪初的医生终于抓住一个"精神病=感染"的成功案例时，他们没有把它当作特例，而是当作范式。Henry Cotton 的拔牙、切胃、摘脾，本质上是把一次真实的发现进行了灾难性的"过拟合"——机器学习里最经典的错误，被应用到人的躯体上。

一个耐人寻味的观察：精神病学的每一次"生物学突破"，都伴随着对身体的进一步殖民。梅毒—GPI 的胜利没有让精神科医生变得更谦逊，反而让他们相信"如果一种精神病能被找到感染源，所有精神病都能"。这是一种典型的"存在性偏差"——他们把幸存的成功样本，误认为是可推广的规律。

二、Wagner-Jauregg 的诺贝尔奖，是"仪式性医学"最完美的化石

给梅毒病人注射疟疾血、让蚊子叮咬被束缚的病人——这项治疗获得诺贝尔奖，不是因为它有效，而是因为它看起来像医学应该有的样子：白大褂、注射器、发烧曲线、显微镜下的病原体。Feynman 后来命名的"货物崇拜科学"（cargo cult science）在这里得到了最惊人的具象化——精神病学模仿了细菌学的所有仪式，却没有细菌学的验证机制。

跨领域连接：这与今天的算法交易、AI 应用、乃至某些管理咨询有惊人的同构性——当一个领域缺乏真正的因果理解，它就会不自觉地放大形式上的科学感来补偿。华尔街的"量化模型"越复杂，越不代表它有预测力；某些医疗 AI 越"深度"，越可能只是在拟合噪声。Wagner-Jauregg 的疟疾疗法与 2008 年的 CDO 定价模型之间，隔着的不是一个世纪，而是同一种认知病理。

三、被忽视的细节：那位工作了 44 年、拔掉几十万颗牙齿的牙医

这是整段对话中最容易被略过、也最深刻的一个人物。他 1916 年进入 Trenton 医院，1960 年退休，坚信 Cotton 应该拿诺贝尔奖。几十万颗牙齿——如果你把它们排成一排，是一个足以引起战栗的意象。他不是恶棍，不是骗子，他是一个"制度内的真信徒"。

这里有一个惊人的跨领域观察：长时间参与一个系统性错误的人，反而比短期参与者更难觉醒。这不是简单的沉没成本，而是一种认知上的自我保护结构——如果他承认 Cotton 错了，他就必须承认自己 44 年的职业生涯是几十万次不必要的伤害。心理系统会自动构建防御，让他把 Cotton 拱上诺贝尔奖的祭坛。

这个模式在任何长周期系统中都会重现：老一代经济学家最难放弃已被证伪的模型；老一代军官最难承认某场战争打错了；老一代产品经理最难承认某个 KPI 体系毁掉了公司。时间和忠诚成正比，而与认知修正能力成反比——这或许是所有大型组织悲剧的根源。

四、一个让人意外的推论：安慰剂效应的强度，是社会等级的函数

对话末尾提到，即使被告知是安慰剂，安慰剂效应对某些人仍然有效。但更深的一层是：安慰剂效应的强度取决于施予者的社会权威。Cotton 之所以能"治愈" 80% 的病人（在报告里），是因为他站在普林斯顿、《纽约时报》、牛津出版社搭建的巨大权威塔之上。他的手术不是普通手术——它是被诺贝尔奖光环、报纸标题、以及"从美国各地涌来的富有病人"共同放大的仪式。

这为一件事提供了尖锐的解释：为什么昂贵的医疗、名校名医、豪华医院的"疗效"经常超过其技术含量所能解释的部分。安慰剂效应不是心理学的边角料——它是社会权威在生物学上的显影剂。而这个显影剂在 1920 年代的精神病学里，把伪科学显影成了国家荣誉。

📝 转录文本

The Full Journey: Asylums, Sterilization, and the Age of Desperate Remedies

Lex: Let's talk about the full journey of everything we've been talking about. So, we mentioned the asylum era that began in the mid-19th century going to the 20th, and we talked about the narratives.

Scull: And we talked about sterilization.

Lex: Sterilization. Yes. And let's look at the insulin shock therapy of 1933 to the 1960s where you were putting patients in deep hypoglycemic comas using large doses of insulin.

Why Psychiatrists Reached for Biology

Scull: Yeah. So, as I mentioned, for psychiatrists who went into the field and were ambitious, but who also wanted to think of themselves as therapeutic agents, to just sit there passively and contain the patients was very unattractive. And so, they looked around for ways in which perhaps biological interventions could be used to ameliorate this condition that they still saw in largely biological terms.

Now, in some ways, one of the crucial early ways in which this thinking went — and which affected a large number of patients — was this. One of the few diagnostic triumphs of psychiatry in the early 19th century, as the profession began to emerge, was that it began to distinguish a group of patients who were deemed to be suffering from something called general paralysis of the insane.

General Paralysis of the Insane (GPI)

That encapsulates two things about what was going on. First of all, paralysis — the gradual loss of motor control, ability to walk, ability to swallow, ability to talk.

Lex: [gasps]

Scull: So, those are primarily what we'd think of these days as neurological issues, but those were bizarre psychiatric symptomatology. These were people who thought they were Napoleon or Jesus Christ or the richest and sexiest man in the world or Mary the mother of God. They were primarily men, but there were also female victims.

At the turn of the 20th century, as many as 25% of the people being admitted to asylums were suffering from general paralysis of the insane, or GPI for short. There were a lot of suspicions about this being connected somehow to sex and to moral dissolution and so forth.

The Syphilis Discovery

But what evolved in the early 20th century was the discovery of the actual origins of this disorder. So, I've said psychiatry's been looking for the underlying pathology that lies behind mental diseases. This was one that, at the Rockefeller Institute, they discovered that the organism that causes syphilis was residing in the brains of the people who were suffering from GPI. This was in fact tertiary stage of syphilis.

Syphilis is still a real public health problem — just like AIDS in the late 19th century, it was everywhere. And when you first contract syphilis, in the primary phase, you have a pain. But then it goes underground. And you think it's gone. And it lurks — the way chickenpox virus lurks and can surface years later. It lurks, it lurks, and it's insidiously damaging.

Sometimes it attacks the heart. And people drop dead of a heart attack in their 40s. "Oh, he died of a — you know, it's a natural heart attack," but in fact it was the syphilis. Or it attacks the central nervous system, the spinal column, the brain. And then you get the paralysis. And then you get also the psychiatric symptomatology.

So when that was discovered, that sort of suggested that mental illness might have an infectious origin.

Two Nobel Prizes in Psychiatry — Both Bizarre

Tertiary syphilis, GPI, went on to win — for somebody who developed a treatment for it — a Nobel Prize, one of only two awarded for psychiatric innovations. One was lobotomy; the other was giving people malaria to cure the syphilis.

Lex: In case people didn't hear that. [snorts] Giving people malaria.

Scull: Yes. In order to cure syphilis.

Wagner-Jauregg's Malaria Therapy

So there was an Austrian doctor, Wagner-Jauregg, who had long thought that fever could be used to cure mental illness. And he tried rat bite fever, he tried giving people typhoid vaccine that creates a fever — to no avail.

And towards the end of World War I, the Italians were fighting in World War I on the side of the British and the Americans and the French. They captured an Italian soldier who had malaria — malaria was endemic in those years in Italy — and they brought him to him, and he extracted the malarial blood and injected it into a series of patients with GPI, with general paralysis of the insane, and claimed it cured them.

We know from later on, when he fessed up, that those claims were wildly exaggerated, but they were widely accepted. And malarial treatment spread to Britain, it spread to Germany, it spread to the United States. Sometimes it was vials of malarial blood, but very often mental hospitals had actual colonies of malarial mosquitoes. So, imagine you're a mental patient and you're put in a straitjacket and you're put in a room and you can't move, and mosquitoes are buzzing around and they bite you and then you develop malaria.

Lex: And he got a Nobel Prize for this.

Scull: Yes, in 1927 he got a Nobel Prize. Because this was a condition that was invariably fatal, and the claim was that somehow the malarial fever worked.

Two Theories, Zero Trials

Now, there are two possible ways. Wagner-Jauregg thought it stimulated the immune system to attack whatever it was causing the insanity. But the other possibility was the following: when you have the malarial parasite in a test tube and you heat the test tube to about 105–106°, it dies. So the idea potentially was that you were sort of burning the parasites out of the brain with this agent.

And because people were pretty unsophisticated about statistics, and because the idea of a controlled trial had not yet come to pass, this treatment was used extensively for a couple of decades. What caused it to stop — and you talk about the progress of science — was the discovery of penicillin, which was a real magic bullet.

Lex: Mhm.

Scull: So, once you had penicillin, you weren't going to continue treating people with malaria. So, it died away. But it was the first such treatment.

The Germ Theory Revolution — And Why It Bypassed Psychiatry

And here's the other way this feeds into the narrative of these desperate remedies that developed in this period between the mid-teens and say 1950. The discovery of the syphilitic origins of general paralysis of the insane occurred at a time when medicine had undergone a profound transformation.

In the late 19th century, the work of Louis Pasteur — who was a chemist, not an MD — and the work of Robert Koch in Germany had uncovered the origins of a variety of diseases and suggested that bacteria were the reason why people sickened. And that led, of course, to a whole series of public health triumphs, because initially it didn't lead to antibiotics, but for a lot of these diseases — even viral diseases like rabies — you could develop a vaccine. And the vaccines were phenomenally effective.

And so that was one way in which the new germ theory of disease transformed medicine and tied it into the laboratory and into science in a new way. And the other was the adaptation of Pasteur's theories by a British surgeon named Lister. Previously, when pus developed post-surgery, people had thought that was a good sign.

Lex: [snorts] [gasps]

Scull: Lister said, "No, I don't think so. This is actually these nasty germs causing this. And so we're going to do antiseptic surgery." So he sprayed carbolic acid on the wounds to try to kill the microbes. Most of his colleagues thought he was nuts — thought this is ridiculous, these microorganisms, you couldn't even see them. Well, you could — with a [microscope]. But Lister prevailed. And eventually we moved from antiseptic surgery to aseptic surgery, which is what we have now, where you try to have a sterilized set of instruments in a sterilized environment so you don't infect things.

Clear Progress vs. Psychiatry's Ambiguity

Lex: By the way, these are definitive examples of progress in medicine.

Scull: Absolutely.

Lex: Penicillin.

Scull: Yes.

Lex: Making sure there's no germs in your surgery.

Scull: Yes.

Lex: So these are all just refreshingly clear examples of progress. The reason I say it's refreshingly clear that there's progress — there's not a refreshingly clear progress in the history of psychiatry. Maybe a few hints.

Scull: Yes. There haven't been the dramatic breakthroughs that I think everybody in the field would hope for. And there's some debate about how powerful what we have done is, and I think it's reasonable to debate that and to also acknowledge that there is important progress, limited as it is.

The Infectious Model Takes Hold

Now you have 25% of the admits to a mental hospital actually suffering from an infectious disease. Medicine in general has now tied its fortunes to the laboratory. The idea that disease is caused by bacteria — we can't yet see viruses — is a very powerful one, and that notion that disease is caused by bacterial infection acquires great momentum. But it hasn't touched psychiatry.

So medicine now has interventions that work, and sometimes quite dramatically. You know, the first patient given diphtheria vaccine — diphtheria causes a leather-like membrane to grow over your throat and you die choking to death. And if you have a child and you watch that child die like that, you will be over it. So when you had something that warded that off, that improved medicine's image dramatically and improved its financial prospects dramatically, particularly as medical training became reformed and more involved with science.

So that hasn't applied to psychiatry — until syphilis comes along. Now we have the model that an infectious agent can cause people's minds to go amok.

Henry Cotton and Focal Sepsis

So, the very person who invents the basic distinctions — kinds of psychoses we still use today, schizophrenia and bipolar disorder — Emil Kraepelin — begins to think, "You know, there may be something infectious about the mental illnesses we're treating." And one of the people he trains is a young psychiatrist from the United States named Henry Cotton, who's also been trained by Adolf Meyer, who is the leading American psychiatrist of the first 40 years of the 20th century.

And when he comes back from Germany, having spent a year there, Meyer secures him a position as head of the New Jersey State Mental Hospital at Trenton. And Cotton is an ambitious reforming man. He wants to bring psychiatry back to medicine. He also wants to chuck out all the old stuff. He doesn't want chains in his hospital. He doesn't want, if he can help it, straitjackets. So that goes away. But nothing seems to change fundamentally. He still isn't curing patients.

And then he comes across this idea of focal sepsis — the idea that low-grade infections can lurk in the body, and what they do is release toxins into the bloodstream and the lymph. And hey, imagine if those toxins get to the brain — what's it going to do? It's going to poison the brain, and the brain is then going to act up.

Lex: Mhm.

Surgical Bacteriology: Teeth, Tonsils, Stomachs

Scull: So, we don't have antibiotics. So what are we going to do about this? Well, we can perhaps locate the bacterial infection, and then we can get rid of it. We can engage in what he calls surgical bacteriology.

So the first obvious target here is teeth. Your teeth look close to your brain. They're often infected. That infection often goes untreated for a time. So, we pull a lot of teeth. Patients don't get better.

Lex: Mhm.

Scull: Maybe the theory's wrong. No. Tonsils. Well, they're getting infected, so we'll remove them. Still don't get better. Well, they're swallowing the bacteria. So we remove stomachs, and we remove spleens, and we remove colons, and we claim to be curing 80% of our patients. And rich patients come from all over America to be treated with this novel treatment.

Lex: Crazy.

Prestige and Death

Scull: Cotton gives a series of lectures at Princeton — the Vanuxem lectures — which are given by Nobel Prize winners. It's a very prestigious series. It's published by Oxford University Press and Princeton University Press. The New York Times hails it as a great breakthrough.

And in reality, 45% of the people who get the abdominal surgery die within a year.

Lex: So they're cutting out stomachs?

Scull: Yeah, he's cutting out stomachs. He says — this is a passage in one of his papers — where he says, "Stomachs are like cement mixers on a construction site and could be dispensed with." And you think, "Oh my god."

If you were released from Trenton and you had no teeth, people immediately knew you were an ex-patient, because the word had spread.

The Dentist Who Believed

And this goes on. Starting in 1916, Cotton drops dead of a heart attack in 1933, but he's succeeded by three people he's trained. They drop the abdominal surgery. They use colonic irrigation, but the teeth and the tonsils keep being pulled. I interviewed the dentist who had come to the hospital in 1916 and must have pulled several hundred thousand teeth. He retired in 1960, which is when that finally stopped. And he was convinced Cotton should have won the Nobel Prize for this.

Why Did Everyone Believe?

Lex: Well, can you just give some intuition — put ourselves in that mind space? I mean, presumably these are smart human beings. Why were they fraudulent in the reporting of how effective it is? Why are all the people that are participating — both the doctors and the general culture?

Scull: It's extraordinary. So obviously, many of the interventions I'm talking about are very powerful interventions conducted by people in white coats and stethoscopes and scalpels.

Lex: Powerful, by the way, by the amount of impact they have on the human body — not powerful in terms of how effective they are.

The Placebo Problem

Scull: Yes — powerful as well in terms of placebo effect. "Look at what I am going to do to you. And yes, it's going to hurt, and it's very [dramatic], but it's going to make you better." So that's always — this is a problem that persisted [into] contemporary psychiatry, trying to figure out how much of the improvement we're seeing is the placebo effect and how much of it is the active effect of whatever we're doing.

Lex: Well, by the way, on that small tangent — let's return to that perhaps often.

Scull: Yes.

Lex: I for one can tell you that, for me — for my mind — the placebo effect, even when you tell me it's placebo, will work.

Scull: Yes.

Lex: But now, if you have combined an actual gigantic operation that is physically, mentally, and every way life-changing — everybody around you in lab coats, all of society is telling you this is going to be life-changing — I get it. That's like the most pure kind of placebo effect.

Scull: It's a placebo effect that comes from both the patient — who wants to be better and wants to believe this is going to make them [better] — and from the person conducting. And it's easy to deceive yourself, to see what you want to see.

item.description:
## 一、精神病学最致命的悖论：**唯一真正的胜利，成为最惨烈失败的模板**
这段对话中隐藏着一个令人毛骨悚然的结构性讽刺——精神病学史上极少数确凿的生物学发现（梅毒螺旋体导致 GPI），恰恰成了随后半个世纪灾难性医疗暴行的"授权文件"。当 20 世纪初的医生终于抓住一个"精神病=感染"的成功案例时，他们没有把它当作**特例**，而是当作**范式**。Henry Cotton 的拔牙、切胃、摘脾，本质上是把一次真实的发现进行了灾难性的"过拟合"——机器学习里最经典的错误，被应用到人的躯体上。
一个耐人寻味的观察：**精神病学的每一次"生物学突破"，都伴随着对身体的进一步殖民**。梅毒—GPI 的胜利没有让精神科医生变得更谦逊，反而让他们相信"如果一种精神病能被找到感染源，所有精神病都能"。这是一种典型的"存在性偏差"——他们把幸存的成功样本，误认为是可推广的规律。
## 二、**Wagner-Jauregg 的诺贝尔奖，是"仪式性医学"最完美的化石**
给梅毒病人注射疟疾血、让蚊子叮咬被束缚的病人——这项治疗获得诺贝尔奖，不是因为它有效，而是因为它**看起来像医学应该有的样子*

item.title: [投资TALK君] ✨【投资TALK君1494期】明明鹰派的沃什，为何美股反弹？又一传统巨头陨落✨20260917#CPI #nvda #美股 #投资 #英伟达 #ai #特斯拉
item.dc:creator: 投资TALK君
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"鹰派反而利多"背后的债券市场"双通道"机制——大多数散户完全看反了

小涛这期最值得咀嚼的洞见，其实藏在一个反直觉的因果链里：当市场真正相信美联储是鹰派的那一刻，长端名义利率反而会下跌。这条链路必须拆成两个通道才看得明白：

  • 通道 A（通胀预期）：鹰派 → 市场相信通胀会被压下去 → break-even 通胀预期下行
  • 通道 B（真实利率）：鹰派 → 市场担心经济增速被牺牲 → 真实利率下行

10年期名义利率 = 通胀预期 + 真实利率，两个通道同时向下，于是"沃什越鹰，长端越跌，黄金越涨，股市越反弹"。

这背后有一个更深层的哲学问题值得点出：当央行的鹰派"credibility（可信度）"足够强时，它甚至不需要真的加息，市场会替它把长端利率打下来。这就是格林斯潘时代所谓的"the Fed doesn't need to do anything, the market does it for them"。沃什如果真的上任，他手里最锋利的武器可能不是政策工具本身，而是"预期锚定"。

二、麦当劳的"优惠券依赖症"——揭示了快消品牌忠诚度的一个残酷真相

小涛把麦当劳的问题定性为"宣发问题、非基本面问题"，我认为这个判断是对的，但它揭示的东西比他讲的更深刻、更颠覆：

麦当劳停发优惠券 → 忠实客户消失 → 这证明了这批"忠实客户"其实从来不是对麦当劳品牌忠诚，而是对"3美元套餐"这个价格锚忠诚。换句话说，麦当劳几十年建立的"brand equity"，在快餐这个赛道里，被证伪为一个"rebate program（返利项目）"。

这里有一个跨领域的意外连接：这个现象和 AI 领域的 RLHF（人类反馈强化学习）机制惊人地相似。大语言模型在训练过程中一旦撤掉奖励信号，行为立刻塌陷回原点——因为所谓"对齐"其实是"外部激励的持续供给"。麦当劳的所谓"品牌忠诚"，就是它对客户的一场长期 RLHF：coupon = reward signal，一旦停发，客户"对齐"随即崩溃。

再往深走一层，这对整个消费股投资框架都是一个警告：你以为你在给"护城河"付估值溢价，你其实可能是在给"促销预算"付溢价。星巴克、Nike 面临的是更根本的品类结构问题；而麦当劳"仅仅是宣发问题"这句话的另一面，其实是"麦当劳承认它没有真正的品牌粘性"。这才是估值可以打到 18 倍的深层原因——市场潜意识里已经在重新计算它的"品牌资产"了。

三、"指数没跌，但市场其实塌方"——从 Intel 供应链数据窥见"信息不对称套利"的结构性机会

小涛提到的三个信号，如果拼在一起看，会浮现一幅大多数投资者从未意识到的市场地图：

  1. AAII 看多比例 28.8%（一年新低，比 3 月关税战当时还低）
  2. 市场参与度极弱，权重股在拖着指数
  3. 大科技 QTD 涨 10%，等权指数只涨 0.3%

这不是一个"接近高点"的市场，这是一个"高点假象下的地下战场"——指数在裸泳，个股在血流成河。这种结构在历史上有一个专业名词叫 "narrow breadth top（窄幅度顶部）"，通常出现在两种情况下：要么大级别顶部前夕，要么大级别底部启动前的最后一次分化。而在此时的情绪面数据（比 3 月还悲观）恰恰指向后者。

更精彩的是 Intel 那条线索——Chips and Wafers 通过韩国出口马来西亚的 HBM 同比 +467% 这个数据点，反推 Intel 封装业务爬坡。这是我想给你的最后一个跨领域连接：

这种"从物流数据反推公司基本面"的方法，本质上和二战期间盟军情报部门通过统计德军坦克序列号来估算德国坦克月产量的"German tank problem"是同一种思维——用系统边缘的可观测信号，去反推系统内部不可观测的真实产能。

现在的 Semianalysis、卫星停车场客流数据、船舶 AIS 数据、进出口海关数据……都是当代版的"tank serial number analysis"。当一个市场的信息效率越来越依赖这类边缘信号时，恰恰意味着传统信息渠道（财报、指引）的边际价值在衰减——这才是真正应该让所有基本面投资者夜不能寐的结构性变化。

一句话结论：这期看似聊三件事（美联储、麦当劳、英特尔），实际上讲了同一件事——在一个"叙事效率"越来越高但"事实效率"越来越低的市场里，唯一的 edge 来自于跨维度的共振：情绪面 × 估值 × 供应链数据 × 债券市场结构。谁能同时读懂 4 张地图，谁就有真正的胜率。

📝 转录文本

开场：进入公司的"内心世界"

昨天那期视频，我们一起走入了沃什的内心世界，大家有没有觉得非常的精彩？觉得精彩的在留言区里面告诉我，要不要我们以后直接去建立一个专题——走入某某人的内心世界，大家觉得好不好？开玩笑啊，没有那么多的人值得我们去进入他的一个内心世界。

今天我不进入一个人内心世界，我们进入一家公司的一个内心世界——麦当劳。

一、警惕"从结果倒推"的思维陷阱

在昨天视频下面，有一条留言让我印象非常的深刻。他说：你在大多数的地方看到的就是——如果当天市场下跌，那解释就是美联储的会议是鹰派的；如果当天市场上涨，那解释就直接倒过去推，那就是美联储是鸽派的。下跌美联储就是鹰派的。

我聊过很多很多很多很多次，一定不要从结果倒推出去，去推这件事情本身的本质到底是什么。如果这么去做的话，我们和写新闻是没有任何差别的。新闻就是这样，新闻永远是从结果出发，给你一个理由去合理化这一个结果。但实际上合理化这个结果之后，对我们没有任何的用处，因为我们不可能拿它去做一个线性外推。

这次美联储会议是最好的一个例子：会议当天市场出现了下跌，如果我们从结果出发，把它解读为是一个鹰派的美联储会议，那我们就根本没有办法理解——为什么周四市场美债收益率反而出现了下跌，美股反而出现了反弹？

这也是我认为我可以给大家带来一些其他地方大家可能看不到的一些内容。因为债券市场本身它是有一定壁垒在那边的，如果不在债券市场里边的话，你是没有办法理解债券市场背后的一个机制，没有办法理解为什么沃什明明是鹰派的，但是第二天长期美债的收益率甚至出现了下跌。希望这样的一些视角能够给大家带来一些帮助。

如果昨天那期视频还不够的话，昨天我是在 APP 上面做了这个直播，然后直播的一个回放现在在 APP 上面，也是针对所有人都开放的。感兴趣或者昨天错过直播内容的话，可以通过画面里面的这个二维码去进行下载，或者直接去商店里面搜索"投资 talk 君"，也可以对这个 APP 进行下载。

欢迎大家来到一个不单只聊新闻、且刚刚进入沃什内心世界的一个专业美股频道，我是市场分析师小涛。大家记得在开始之前留言、点赞、加转发。

二、周四资产价格走势

废话不多说，我们先来看一下周四资产价格的走势：

  • 美债收益率：两年期和十年期分别下跌了 7 个基点和 9 个基点。为什么会出现下跌，稍后我有张图和大家分享一下，主要我们去看一下十年期美债收益率为什么下跌。
  • 黄金：10 年期美债收益率的下跌，也使得黄金在周四出现了一个反弹。
  • 比特币：上涨的幅度并不大，但是我认为如果黄金可以持续出现反弹的话，比特币也会跟着黄金去反弹。中间可能会有一个滞后，然后可能会走出两者之间的一些差距，但是我认为两者的方向应该是一致的。
  • TLT：上涨了 1.1%，长期美债收益率反而出现了下跌。

为什么加息，长期美债收益率反而出现了下跌？如果大家有这一段时间有一直 follow 我这个逻辑的话，不会对于今天债券市场的这个走势感到任何的意外。

三大指数这边都出现了比较大幅度的反弹：标普 500 涨 1.1%，纳指 1.7%，道指 0.6%。

板块这边可以看到，基本上所有的板块都出现了上涨。两个板块国防下跌了，然后保险板块出现小幅下跌。涨幅最好的板块来自于芯片，3.4%——高贝塔动能板块。

三、半导体板块：悲观情绪已被提前定价

芯片板块的这个反弹，其实我在周三的 X 上面，有别人问我：你是不是认为整个硬件板块、整个半导体板块，市场的一个悲观情绪面在这一次会议之前已经被定价了、已经被提前定价？我的回答是：是的。

虽然我当时说了，我对于猜市场的这个底部不是那么的准确，但是起码我个人的看法我是非常的坚定——我认为半导体板块现在的估值就是便宜的。即使在昨天美联储会议之后，我 X 上的这个观点也非常的明确：我说在这个点位或者这个点位以下，都是一个买点，直到财报之前。

四、市场参与度：指数背后的"隐形塌方"

最后这张图里我想聊的是，在周四出现反弹之后，你看：

  • 大科技反弹的幅度非常的好，1.8%
  • 等权指数只有 0.5%

你可以看一下 QTD 整个七月份到现在为止，等权指数其实相当的弱，只有 0.3%。前期大科技股反弹的幅度非常的好，将近 10%，等权指数相对比较弱。

你可以看到 QTD 到现在为止，反而大多数的板块是出现了下跌。虽然指数没怎么下跌，但是大多数的板块都出现了下跌。这最终就导致了——你去看标普 500 离新高其实没有那么的远，但实际上整个市场的参与度的跌幅却非常的大。

能够理解吗？说明大多数的个股在下跌，但是权重股把指数拖在那边。

五、AAII 情绪指标：一年新低

讲到了市场参与度，其实有另外两个指标和市场的参与度有一点异曲同工之妙，也是去衡量当下市场的这个情绪面。市场的参与度它其实是一个技术性的指标，今天和大家分享的叫 AAII 投资者的情绪面指标。

这一个情绪面指标其实它是一个调查出来的结果，就是去调查当下市场到底是乐观的还是悲观的，调查的是个人投资者。AAII 的这一组指数每周四会公布，然后周三是数据截止的日期，周四公布了这一周的数据。

这一周数据出来之后，我们来看一下：图里白色这条线是看多人的比例，周四这个数据录得是 28.8%——只有 28.8% 的人在当下的市场里面是乐观的。这一个百分比是过去一年以来的一个新低。这一个指数在周三所录得的数据，比今年的 3 月份关税战当时还要低。当时的关税战是在 31% 左右，周三的数据是 28.8%。

这组数据和市场参与度这个数据有一点不一样的是，因为这组数据每周公布一次，所以它的更新频率不是那么的高，但是从结果去看它还是符合的。那我也不希望把大家把这组数据就当做是一个唯一的指标，可以把它理解为和市场参与度是一样的——它是一个模糊的正确。

如果说我们有不同的指标都指向当下市场是在一个悲观情绪下，它就足够了。我说每一个指标，只要这个指标本身能够帮我们去提高胜率，那么无论是投资的胜率还是交易的胜率，有另外一个维度进来之后，不同维度不同的指标出现共振，那这个共振是增加了我们这一笔投资或者交易赚钱的概率，这就足够了。它永远是一个模糊正确，永远不可能有任何一个指标或者两个指标结合在一起能够 100% 保证我们这一笔交易就是赚钱的。

图里蓝色这条线是标普 500 的指数。我们可以看到，虽然离最高点不是那么的远（跌幅可能就 2%、3% 的距离），但是现在市场参与度在一个低位，所以情绪面现在确确实实在一个低位。今年的 3 月份的时候，可以看到标普 500 的点位是在 6400 点以下，那当时整个市场乐观的人这个比例其实也是非常的低，在 30% 左右。

既然有看多的人的比例，也会有看空人的比例，对吧？AAII 调查者这个指数它是有看多的人比例、看空人的比例，然后中性的比例。看空的比例也去到了过去一年的一个新高——看多是过去一年的新低，看空是过去一年的新高。这就说明当下市场情绪没有多么的悲观，所以不要感到意外，这些指标本身相对都是比较客观的一些数据。

六、10 年期美债收益率的拆解：真实利率 + 通胀预期

然后我们回到债券市场这边，来看一下 10 年期美债收益率。把 10 年期美债收益率拆开来去看：

10 年期美债收益率 = 真实利率 + 通胀预期

图里白色这条线是 break-even 通胀预期，蓝色这条线是真实利率。

观察一：过去一个交易日两者同步下跌

第一点是我右边红色框框之内。红色框框之内我们可以看到是从周三的收盘到周四的收盘。在这一个区间里边，白色这条线也下降、蓝色这条线也下降。这说明什么？ 这说明在整个周四的交易日里边，我们看到不单是通胀的预期往下降，真实利率也往下降。

在这种情况下，十年期美债收益率下降了 9 个基点，所以黄金出现上涨是非常合理的结果。

当通胀预期出现下降，说明市场其实对于沃什鹰派的态度他是买单的——因为市场相信沃什是鹰派的，所以能够压制通胀，所以通胀的预期往下降。白色这条线往下降是在期待之内的。我昨天在 X 上面我也说过，我的期待是接下去 break-even 会往下降的，但是下降的幅度有多少，稍后另外一张图和大家分享。

那蓝色这条线真实利率往下降，这背后就有很多理由了。如果一定要去套这个结果的话，我们可以理解为：因为市场知道沃什是鹰派的，那所以一个鹰派的美联储，它未来有可能会伤害到什么？会伤害到经济增速。真实利率一部分是反映了经济增速。如果经济增速因为沃什的鹰派而出现下降的话，那 10 年期美债的真实利率就会出现下降。当真实利率下降的时候，黄金就会出现上涨。

观察二：周三下午 2 点后的即时反应

第二点是我这边所圈出来一个红色圈圈之内。红色圈圈之内是在周三 2 点之后，白色这条线的走势非常明显——十年期通胀的预期在 2 点之后是往下降的。也就是市场明显 get 到了沃什当时的态度是鹰派的。

包括 2 点之后美联储宣布加息，宣布加息，市场也看到了美联储的这个态度。美联储这个鹰派态度表现出来之后，通胀的预期自然就会下降，因为市场知道美联储如果是鹰派的话，将会把通胀给压下去。

展望：白线还有下行空间，蓝线是个问号

同样还是前面那张图，如果我们放到过去一年的走势——图里白色这条线通胀预期，经过周三的下跌之后，来到了 2.316。我期待白色这条线通胀预期还会有下行的空间。前段时间 7 月份的低点是在 2.2%，所以从现在的位置可能还会有向下 12 个基点的空间。

然后蓝色这条线真实利率这一块，我就打了一个问号在那边。因为影响到真实利率背后的因素会比较的多：

  • 美联储的态度本身
  • 或者说市场认为美联储的态度本身对于未来经济增速的影响
  • 或者说贝森特的态度

如果说贝森特在中期选举之前，他的态度是非常坚定的话，那蓝色这条线也会有下降的空间。

如果蓝色这条线下降、白色这条线也下降，就代表 10 年期美债的名义利率一定下降。如果名义利率下降的话，对于股市、黄金、比特币，都是一个利好。

七、个股一：英特尔——从供应链数据验证基本面

OK，然后就来聊个股。那在我们进入麦当劳的内心世界之前，我们先来聊另外一家个股——英特尔。

大家知道英特尔是我第一大的仓位，所以今天因为英特尔上涨的幅度比较的大，所以对我整体投资组合的贡献也比较的大，差一点点就再次账户去破了一个新高了。

基本面 edge 的两种来源

我想聊英特尔的是，如果我们去关注这个市场的话，其实我们对于一个标的的 edge（优势）可以来自于两方面：

第一方面是对于基本面判断本身。这个判断很多时候从我个人的角度，我不大会去经常做更新，因为短期基本面不会出现非常大的改变。

另外一种就是对基本面的研究，比如说过去这段时间市场非常流行的是对于整个半导体板块的供应链去进行摸底。如果你摸到底，或者你背后有这个渠道的话，你会获得一手信息，对于你投资交易这块可能会有一个帮助。

HBM 出口马来西亚数据 → 英特尔封装业务爬坡

我今天和大家举个例子：这条推是来自于 Chips and Wafers，它其实是 Semianalysis 旗下的一个账号。这个账号在 8 月 16 日的时候就已经有聊到：他说在韩国那边，HBM 会往外运，往外运之后要进行封装。而 HBM 往外运的这一个地点已经慢慢的从增速这个角度去看，马来西亚超过了台湾。

  • 运到台湾去是给什么？运到台湾去是给台积电进行封装。
  • 运到马来西亚去背后代表什么？因为英特尔在马来西亚有一个封装厂，所以运到马来西亚去说明英特尔在封装这一块的营收接下去会进行一个爬坡，或者产能会进行一个爬坡。

如果说你知道这一类消息，或者你提前知道这一类消息，那你可以去布局英特尔。这就是如果你对于整个行业供应链有一个摸底或者有这个优势在那边的话，这是做基本面的一种。

我的信息来自财报电话会

但是对于我个人来说，我没有这个渠道。那么但是对于我来说，我提早就已经知道了这条消息——这是在上一个季度财报里面管理层自己说的，他们接下去营收增速有三个来源，其中一个来源就是在封装这一块，管理层说的非常的明确。

所以某种程度我无论是 Chips and Wafers 在 8 月 16 日所发的那条，还是在周四的时候他又发了另外一条——具体的数据出来了：从出口数据同比增速可以看到增长了 467%，体量达到了 1.6 亿美金。所以这条新闻本身对于我在基本面上的判断，它是一个验证。

这个基本面的判断其实并不是来自于我主观的判断，而是管理层在上一个季度财报里面就已经告诉我，我选择相信管理层，然后管理层通过执行力现在做出了这个结果。但是如果你没有听财报，然后比较专注于对于供应链的摸底，你如果有这个信息渠道的话也可以，你会提早获得这一类的数据。

八、个股二：麦当劳——不是宏观问题，是营销问题

OK，最后我们一起来进入麦当劳的这个内心世界。

其实我今天不是特意要聊麦当劳，正好我看到了这条新闻，然后我记得在前段时间一期视频的留言下面，有人让我去聊一下麦当劳。其实麦当劳我可能在几周之前、一个月之前我有聊过，我认为麦当劳其实是一个买点。那现在这个价格其实比一个月之前更低一些，那我们继续对麦当劳的基本面来做一个更新。

新闻：麦当劳推出新价值战略

我看到这条新闻是：麦当劳准备推出它新的价值战略，以重振美国的销售。

我上次去听了麦当劳上一个季度的财报，麦当劳现在当下的一个情况是什么——并不是现在消费者非常的弱，而是它的宣发策略出现了问题。

它以前的一种宣发方式是：会发库胖（coupon）出去，发电子库胖或者发纸质的库胖出去，有 3 块钱的 meal、有 5 块钱的 meal。但是他突然之间停掉了。停掉之后你马上发现：原来麦当劳非常忠诚的这个客户不来了——也就是这一部分客户原来是非常依赖于这些库胖的，但是你库胖不发的话，他们就不来了。

所以麦当劳股价的下跌，并不是因为宏观。你说宏观有一些因素嘛，有一点点因素，但主要还是公司自己本身策略的问题。

内部动作：换掉美国 marketing 主管

所以麦当劳他们在上一次财报会里面，他们把美国的那个管 marketing 的主管已经开了。

我觉得麦当劳股价的低迷，其实如果你去和星巴克去做对比、或者和 Nike 去做对比的话，它这个问题本身，如果只是宣发问题本身的话，这个问题其实不是那么的严重。因为当他把宣发重新调整回来之后，以前丢失的这些客户，我认为麦当劳还是可以争取回来的。

只要你的质量并没有变，然后你的 value proposition（价值主张）、性价比仍然在那边的话，我认为这部分客户还是会回归的。 因为通常来说快餐这一块的客户是没有非常大的一个忠诚度在那边的，唯一有的一个忠诚度就是你这个产品本身对于他们非常的有吸引力。一旦现在大家对于价格又非常的敏感，你的价格如果没有优势的话，那马上就转到其他一些快餐身上。

所以麦当劳自己公司内部本身看到了这个问题，接下去也现在已经推出了新的价值策略去解决这个问题。我认为很快公司内部应该可以把这一部分以前犯的错误给去修补。

估值维度：Forward PE 18.19 倍——多年低位

那我们从其他的维度来看一下麦当劳。第一个维度就是估值了。

Forward PE 截止到周四的收盘在 18.19 倍。 其实 18.19 倍已经是过去好几年以来的一个相当低的位置。上一次比现在还要低的位置是在 2020 年，再上一次的话要追溯到 2016 年了。所以现在麦当劳这个位置绝对是在一个非常低的位置。

Risk / Reward 分析

我举个例子：我们假设——因为现在麦当劳起码还是在基本面的左侧，就是市场现在也没有去定价它基本面会出现一个回归，所以现在你要去买入的话，一定是我们知道是在基本面的左侧。

如果在左侧，你思考一下，最坏的情况是什么？ 那在基本面没有变得更加糟的情况下，最坏的情况可能估值还可以往下跌。继续往下跌，下面一个支撑位从估值这个角度去看，下面的支撑位在哪？可能就是在 16 倍——16 倍就是 2020 年的低点。有没有可能低到那么低的位置呢？我这边打上非常大的一个问号。

  • 从 18.1 倍再跌到 17 倍左右，我认为是合理的。
  • 能不能跌到 16 倍，或者情绪面非常低低到 16 倍，我还是要打上一个问号。
  • 你现在这个位置建仓，然后下面加仓的位置在 17 倍左右，我认为是合理的。

那我们在投资一个标的的时候，我们必须要知道 risk 和 reward。Reward 是什么？ 我认为这个 reward 就是它估值的回归。你可以看到我这边画了一个上区间是在 26 倍。假设你不会回到 26 倍，24 倍吧——24 倍其实是过去好几年一个比较中性的位置。

  • 从现在的 18 倍回归到 24 倍，你的估值可以上涨多少？差不多正好是 30% 左右。
  • 在这个基础上，如果还可以有 EPS 的一些叠加的话，那你的上区间就是在 30% 至 35% 左右。
  • 再上一个区间是从 24 倍到 26 倍，那你的上区间就会抬升到 40% 甚至以上。

所以理论上来说：

下行区间约 10%（18 倍跌到 16.3 倍），上行区间约 30%–40%。

所以我认为麦当劳现在其实是有一个 risk / reward 在那边的，以现在的这个价位。

我个人的看法是，我认为麦当劳是可以扭转这个趋势，因为它不是一个非常严重基本面上的问题。所以如果现在有一些比如说想去布局一些价值股的话，麦当劳这个标的本身，我认为现在是可以考虑的。

营收增速维度：结构性并无问题

然后另外一个维度这边是他们的营收增速。可以看到：

  • 24 年营收增速 2%
  • 23 年 10%（因为 23 年比 2022 年会有一个基数效应在那边，2022 年是 0%，所以 23 年突然之间 10%）
  • 平均增速在 5% 左右
  • 25 年回归到正常增速 4%
  • 26 年市场预期 5%
  • 27 年 5%
  • 28 年 4%

所以麦当劳的问题它不是非常严重的基本面问题，只是它在营销这一块以前犯了一个比较严重的错误。

技术面：周 K 已经超卖

再来看另外一个维度——技术面。

  • 日 K 线这个角度去看，现在还没有进入一个超卖的区间。
  • 周 K 线这一块，RSI 现在已经进入了一个超卖的区间。上一次进入超卖的区间是在 2023 年的 10 月份，已经是在两年之前了。
  • 我这边画了一条横线，应该是在 234 左右吧，下面可以看到有一个比较明显的支撑在那边。

麦当劳快速总结

  • 基本面有没有问题？是有问题的，但不是大问题。主要是在宣发这一块，公司内部对于人员进行了处理，策略上也进行了调整。接下去就是看他们的执行力，能不能通过策略上的调整把基本面带回来。基本面本身我不认为是太大的问题，但是市场并不买账——市场一定要看到结果之后才会买账，所以最后一定要体现在他们的财报里边。所以现在仍然是基本面的左侧。
  • 估值：现在已经是在过去几年的一个相当低的位置。18 倍左右这个 PE 我认为是相当低的，下区间可能就是在 17 倍左右，从现在的话再往下 5% 左右。即使你在现在这个位置从估值角度去开仓，17 倍的时候去加仓，我认为性价比其实比较高。当然你是需要耐心的——这个耐心就是公司必须要通过策略上的转变最后体现到财报数据里边，让市场去买账。如果估值回归到 24 倍的市盈率，比起现在 18 倍有 30% 的上涨空间。
  • 技术面共振：短期日 K 线还没有超卖。如果说日 K 线也超卖、周 K 线也超卖，非常的好，Perfect——多个维度出现共振，增加了赚钱的概率。周 K 线现在已经是超卖了，估值也是在一个低位，然后基本面如果你坚信这家公司管理层可以把它带回来的话，那其实麦当劳这家公司本身，我认为已经是一个买点了。

九、投资心法：合理的期待

最后有一点我想强调——我们每投资一家公司，我们必须要知道对于这家公司的期待一定要合理。你不能抱着不合理的期待。比如说你买入麦当劳，你认为麦当劳的股价要翻一倍，这是完全不合理的期待。

这两天有人在 X 上问我：为什么亚马逊那么的弱？亚马逊那么的弱我还能够理解，从最高点回调了 10%。但有人问我为什么微软那么的弱，我没办法理解——微软其实现在的走势是非常的强。它从上一次财报发布完之后一波大涨，之后又出现了几天的上涨，然后到现在一直在横盘。当你出现了一波大涨之后一直在横盘，其实是一个非常强的走势。

标普 100 假设平均一年上涨 10%，大科技一年如果能够上涨 20%，已经是非常好的回报——因为大科技的贝塔才多少，1.3、1.4、1.5、1.6。所以标普上涨 10%，通常情况下大科技就是上涨 14%、15%。那么大科技如果能够上涨 20%、25%，已经是非常好的回报了。

所以回报的期待一定要合理。也不能说你买入大科技和买入麦当劳一样，我期待它在未来一年涨 50%、翻一倍——不可能，或者这不是一个大概率的事件。

如果你选择今天买入麦当劳，或者你认为麦当劳确实是值得去布局的，那对于麦当劳未来这个回报预期也一定要合理。包括麦当劳的仓位在你整体投资组合里面它的定位是什么、它和其他标的的相关性到底是什么，这些必须要清楚。

十、Seeking Alpha 活动

最后，今天要提醒大家的是 Seeking Alpha 他们的一个活动：

  • 首先是 Seeking Alpha Alpha Picks 他们一个量化选股策略，现在有一个免费的试用期，然后首年的订阅费立即节省 50 美金。
  • 另外，他们的量化选股策略又推出了一个新的背后标的，这个量化选股策略叫做 Quant Growth Income，里边所针对的一些标的都是防守属性比较强的，它的贝塔都是小于 1 的，都是属于一些价值股的量化选股策略。如果说对于这些防守性比较强的标的感兴趣的话，可以参考一下 Seeking Alpha 他们新的这个策略。这个策略本身现在也是首年会有 50 美金的优惠。

我会把这两个订阅的链接（包括这个 combo）会放到置顶的留言里边。

item.description:
## 一、"鹰派反而利多"背后的债券市场"双通道"机制——大多数散户完全看反了
小涛这期最值得咀嚼的洞见，其实藏在一个反直觉的因果链里：**当市场真正相信美联储是鹰派的那一刻，长端名义利率反而会下跌**。这条链路必须拆成两个通道才看得明白：
- **通道 A（通胀预期）**：鹰派 → 市场相信通胀会被压下去 → break-even 通胀预期下行 - **通道 B（真实利率）**：鹰派 → 市场担心经济增速被牺牲 → 真实利率下行
10年期名义利率 = 通胀预期 + 真实利率，两个通道**同时向下**，于是"沃什越鹰，长端越跌，黄金越涨，股市越反弹"。
这背后有一个更深层的哲学问题值得点出：**当央行的鹰派"credibility（可信度）"足够强时，它甚至不需要真的加息，市场会替它把长端利率打下来**。这就是格林斯潘时代所谓的"the Fed doesn't need to do anything, the market does it for them"。沃什如果真的上任，他手里最锋利的武器可能不是政策工具本身，而是"预期锚定"。
