item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"高铁到无处"是一面照妖镜：它照出的不是无能，而是激励结构的完美运行

大多数人看加州高铁的第一反应是"政府真蠢"。但一个更令人不安的观察是：从系统内部人员的激励来看，这个项目运行得极其"成功"。

  • 承包商每天不工作赚 17 万美元，一个月 500 万，最近一次"延误赔偿"和解金额是 5 亿美元——"不干活"比"干活"利润率更高。
  • 加州至今没买真正的列车。视频中 Nick 的解读很尖锐："因为他们自己也知道永远不会有火车跑在这条铁轨上。"
  • 每年 10 亿美元的稳定拨款，是一个持续 20 年的现金流机器，它对既得利益者而言不是失败，是"年金"。

系统的荒谬只在"这是为了修一条铁路"这个前提下才成立。一旦你把它重新定义为"一个把公共资金稳定转移给特定承包商的合法管道"，一切参数——工期、预算、变更单——都变得完全合理。这正是经济学家 Mancur Olson 在《国家兴衰探源》里说的"分利联盟"：项目越大越难完成，越能维持越多人的饭碗，因此"完不成"才是均衡解。

二、跨领域连接：加州高铁 = 一个"反向 SpaceX"，它的失败逻辑与硅谷的成功逻辑同源

一个出人意料的角度：加州高铁和 SpaceX 其实是同一套加州体制的两个极端产物。

  • SpaceX 的核心机制是"reusable rocket"——每一次发射都必须验证经济性，失败即出局，成功即压缩下一次的边际成本。
  • 加州高铁的核心机制是"reusable delay"——每一次延误都变成一次新的赔付，成功即出局（因为项目结束现金流终止），失败即被写入下一轮预算。

两者面对同样的加州劳动力、同样的物流、同样的监管环境，产出却截然相反。差别不是"公 vs 私"这么表面——差别在于反馈闭环的方向：SpaceX 的失败会反噬发起人的资产负债表，高铁的失败会反哺发起人的资产负债表。

这就解释了一个视频里没直接说的事：为什么硅谷这批人（Chamath、Sacks、Jason）会如此激烈地捧 Nick Shirley？因为他们本能地识别出——加州高铁不是"另一个赛道"，而是他们所在赛道的镜像负片。捧 Nick，等于捧他们自己商业模式的合法性基础。

三、更深的隐藏模式：Nick Shirley 现象是"注意力资本"对"制度性资本"的第一次结构性反攻

大多数人把 Nick 定位成"新一代记者"，但这个定位太小了。真正发生的事情是：

当传统机构（60 Minutes、Frontline）的"制度性资本"被政治站队掏空之后，出现了一种可以绕过它的新型资本——"注意力资本"。 一个 24 岁、由妈妈掌镜、没受过任何新闻训练的年轻人，凭什么能让加州立法机构专门为他起草一部法律（AB2624，被戏称为"Nick Shirley 法案"）？

答案是：他的边际调查成本趋近于零，而传统机构的边际调查成本因为编辑、法务、广告主关系变得极高。这就产生了一个反常识的现象——在同样的事实面前，一个人的力量可能大于一个百年机构，因为他不需要维护"机构的生存"这个附加约束。

这里有一个令人震惊的对称： - 加州立法者用一部法律试图关闭他的话筒——这恰恰证明了他们已经承认：一个 YouTuber 的曝光效力 > 州司法系统的常规执法效力。 - 而 Chamath 主动提出每月赞助几千美元、建议他招研究员和保镖——这是风险资本第一次以"支持独立调查记者"作为可投资标的。

更深的含义："注意力资本"正在开始承担过去只有"制度性资本"能做的事——纠错、审计、问责。这不是新闻业的复兴，这是新闻业的解构与重装。就像 Uber 之于出租车公司、Airbnb 之于酒店——审计和问责正在被"分布式化"。

而这里埋着一个隐忧，也是节目最后 Jason 说漏嘴的一句："你还在和你所处的注意力机制作斗争……在某个点上你的激励是——我必须做一些能获得点击的事"。当注意力资本取代制度性资本承担公共审计功能时，它同样会被自己的激励结构扭曲——只是扭曲的方向和 60 Minutes 不同：不是"选择性沉默"，而是"选择性戏剧化"。

这就是为什么 Nick 说自己"晚上睡不着觉想的是——怎么让骗子不至于开门就朝我开枪"。他不只是在和骗子博弈，他也在和自己的商业模式博弈。这才是这个故事真正未完的部分。

📝 转录文本

开场：15 亿美元能造出什么？

Hey besties, if you were given $15 billion, what could you build? The next PayPal, perhaps the next SpaceX, the next Google, or would you build a high-speed rail?

This is the California high-speed rail that goes to absolutely nowhere. And I mean absolutely nowhere, I mean literally nowhere. This is all California has to show for $15 billion in 18 years of work.

In 2008, they said they were going to connect Los Angeles to San Francisco. To this date, they have connected literally nothing. And now to finish this project, they're estimated it's going to cost a hundred to $200 billion.

And funny enough, in 2008, China also created their own high-speed rail. And they've connected the whole entire country of China, over 30,000 miles. Here in California, they haven't connected a single town.

We're going to be breaking down this entire thing from start to finish to show you guys what is actually happening with the California high-speed rail. Let's get into it.

现场调查：世界最贵的"现代巨石阵"

Now, let's go talk to somebody who knows a lot about the California high-speed rail.

Q: What's the truth about the high-speed rail here inside of California?

Well, we call it California high-speed rail, but all we have is concrete and rebar and about $15 billion spent. It currently is right now the most expensive infrastructure project happening in the world today.

The original estimates for California high-speed rail was $33 billion. It then jumped to $126 billion, and now the newest estimate is $236 billion.

This project is on track for one thing, and that is to be the third most expensive infrastructure project in the history of the world. Number one is the interstate project of the 1950s. Number two is the International Space Station. And now it is California high-speed rail.

The difference between those three projects is: you can drive on I-5 or you can go on I-80 and drive across the entire country. You can go to outer space. We will never ride California high-speed rail.

So it goes from there all the way to right here. This is where it ends. It is probably the most expensive piece of concrete known to man, and often referred to here in the Central Valley as a modern-day Stonehenge.

Q: How come they continue to say that they're going to continue to build the high-speed rail when there's actually proof that it is quite literally impossible?

Governor Newsom, in a video himself from 2016, I believe, actually admitted to all of us in a private video that he doesn't believe that this project will ever be done in our lifetime. He said that:

"Okay, the facts seem overwhelming that this project is not going to materialize in our lifetime."

钱去哪了：变更单、延误赔偿与"没买的火车"

Q: And now this is a result of over $15 billion. Who's taken the $15 billion? And where's the $15 billion gone if this is all that they have to show for?

One-third of the entire cost of California high-speed rail has gone to this part called change-order delays, because they didn't know where the infrastructure was and/or how to build this actual train.

Contractors that got awarded a parcel to work on are owed $170,000 a day, $5 million a month for every single day they can't work. We just settled here in California very recently, in February, the largest settlement in a delay settlement for over half a billion dollars. Because a contractor couldn't work on the actual project, they were owed a half a billion dollars.

Q: What are some of the biggest examples of waste, fraud, and just complete incompetence by the government when you see this high-speed rail?

California was supposed to buy the actual trains—the trains that would be considered high-speed rail. The state didn't buy the trains, my opinion, because they know that there will never be a train on these tracks.

Q: So, California has not even bought the trains yet?

No. If we would just buy one-way tickets at current ridership between San Francisco and LA, which is the goal of California high-speed rail, we could subsidize free tickets one way for the next 150 years. Now, with the new estimate that California high-speed rail is going to be $236 billion, we could subsidize one-way tickets between San Francisco and LA for the next 300 years.

So, to me, it would make more sense for all of us to just buy the flights from San Francisco to LA than it would be to build a train or whatever this is and spend more money doing that. I mean, it doesn't make any sense mathematically.

走上路轨：没有铁轨的"高铁"

Now, we're on top of the high-speed rail, and there's not any rail that has been placed. It's actually just a bunch of cement. The high-speed rail to nowhere. That's what they should call it, actually.

And despite the California high-speed rail appearing to be impossible to finish, California has allocated $1 billion a year to finish the project, while they actually need anywhere from 100 to $200 billion to finish it.

And the high-speed rail even becomes more interesting when you realize how impossible it is the further along the alignment you go. And later we'll be confronting the senator who's over the oversight committee for the transportation inside of California.

We then saw some train tracks where the hub of the high-speed rail is supposed to be.

— Hello. — Hey. — How you guys doing? Is this the high-speed rail though? — Uh, no. So you can't be out. This is high— — Not the high-speed rail. Where's the—going to be the hub for the high-speed rail? — I'm not sure. — You don't know where the hub is going to be for the high-speed rail? — No.

荒诞现场：一边修高铁，一边在铁轨上盖房子

And despite these guys saying this is not the hub for the high-speed rail—which it really is—we then went down the alignment and this is what we found.

So, this location right here was actually bought in 2006 for developers to develop this land. And then they set forth the plan to actually go through with the high-speed rail in 2008. In order for the high-speed rail to actually happen, they're going to have to go through and buy each and every single one of these houses that is currently being built.

Keep in mind: right now they're building the high-speed rail while these people are building houses on the alignment.

Let's go talk to a city manager right now.

Q: How is it possible right now that here in California you have a government who is spending billions upon billions of dollars for this high-speed rail, meanwhile a construction site is right here where they're building houses on where that high-speed rail is supposed to go?

We don't really know. Typically government buys all of the alignment up front. That way you don't have cost of buying it once it's developed—like this will bring it up 10 or 11 times what bare land value would be. So, we don't really know. Communication is pretty sparse, so we're left mostly in the dark.

Q: Do you think that this high-speed rail has just been some sort of fantasy for the people inside of Sacramento and the politicians of California?

Look, you've got a project that duplicates Amtrak's current service route. I will tell you from a ground perspective, we don't understand why they're sticking two rail lines next to each other that are going to serve the same areas.

Q: And how many more cases of this do you think are inside of this alignment for the high-speed rail?

I don't think this is atypical. I think this has happened quite a bit up and down the valley.

农民的账：被切成两半的百年农场

California actually abandoned the route from San Francisco to Los Angeles. Now they're focusing from Merced to Bakersfield. And so the high-speed rail will actually not even be servicing people from Los Angeles to San Francisco.

The high-speed rail bridge ends over there. It continues over here onto this road, but as you'll see, it then has to go through a bunch of farmland just like this. Now, they have the road right here for the high-speed rail, but in other locations, do they have it?

We're going to go speak with the farmer right now.

Q: Now, we're in the middle of an orchard right now. How will the farmers be affected from the high-speed rail?

Ranches that have been contiguous for hundreds of years will now be split. And that requires you now having to travel to both sides, right? Your infrastructure has to be pulled from one side to the other—whether it be irrigation, power supplies—and even just operationally, it's just going to make everything real inconvenient.

Q: When California brought about the plan for the high-speed rail, did you guys vote on it or did you guys have any say-so with it, or do you even think it's going to happen?

You know, all the voters had a chance to vote and it passed. But it was very vague on the ballot. No one knew where it was going to go. To me, they're putting it in all the wrong spots. It was to serve two different populations—in the north of the state and the south. And where they're deciding to put it, it's going to impact an area that didn't need the high-speed rail to begin with.

Q: They're allocating millions and billions of dollars to this each and every single year. And now they're saying they're going to need almost a hundred billion dollars more, if not $200 billion. What could farmers of California do if they had a hundred billion invested into them?

Oh man, it could revolutionize the state. I mean, agriculture has been the backbone of this state since its founding. And we're not investing in water infrastructure. We're not investing in energy infrastructure. And it's just—it's sad, because we're worried about a train that's going to serve a small sector of the population. And what really needs to be done is something that's going to be good for all of us in the state.

Q: So pretty soon we could see a high-speed rail come right through here where all these almonds are at. And people are going to be suffering because of it?

Yes. And there'll probably be no one on the train.

直面参议员：一份 20 年、200 亿美元的承诺

Now, we came here to Sacramento to go speak with the people at the California High-Speed Rail Authority office. It is 4:09 right now, and we just went inside and nobody's here.

— Hallelujah. — Really? — Said they're open.

They close at 5:00 p.m. However, they are not here. But we are going to go speak with a senator who just approved and passed a bill that's going to give $1 billion for the next 20 years to the California High-Speed Rail Authority. We're going to go talk to him and see why he approved that.

— Senator Cortese, how are you doing? — Good. — My name is Nick Shirley. We're doing a little investigation on the high-speed rail. We just want to ask: what made you want to secure $1 billion for the next 20 years for the high-speed rail? — I believe it's a good long-term commitment that we need to make. — And do you think that's actually ever going to happen here inside the state of California? — It is happening. Have you been there? — Yeah, I actually have. — All right. Well, then you know it's happening. — And there's actually not a single piece of rail or track that's been laid. — They're getting ready to do that right now. — And do you think in 20 years the high-speed rail will be done, as promised it's going to be done in 2020? — It might be, might not. — Gavin Newsom even said in a private video like it's not even possible essentially. — I have a lot of transportation projects I've worked on for 20 years that are just finally getting started, and they're all worth it. — And do you believe, as a chair of the Senate Transportation Committee, do you believe the High-Speed Rail Authority has been sufficiently accountable for the increase and delays that have taken place with the high-speed rail? — Well, we're trying to hold them accountable. — And what can you give to people to make them believe that the high-speed rail is actually going to be built and finished in our lifetime or in your lifetime? — It's not my commitment. My commitment is: it's the greatest economic development project in the country, and people should be embracing that all the way to the federal government. There's no other economic development project that even comes close to that in this country. And it's a shame that certain people in the country aren't taking that seriously. So that's how we get things done—is when the federal government, the state government work together. Build dams, build bridges, build highways, build high-speed rail. That's what needs to happen. — And you do believe that we'll see the finish of the high-speed rail in our lifetime? — There's 21 construction projects going on right now with thousands of workers. So you'll see it get done.

Besties, don't be like the high-speed rail.

All-In Podcast 现场：欢迎 Nick Shirley

— Please welcome Nick Shirley. — Fuck yeah. Fuck yeah. What's up, bro? — Hey man. — Sacks, this is your guy. Get in there.

加州立法反击：AB2624 —— "Nick Shirley 法案"

Sacks: Wow. Uh, maybe a good place to start actually is that California was so afraid of what you're doing—exposing their fraud—that they actually passed a law to stop you from doing your investigations and, you know, your videos where you actually show up at these places that are stealing taxpayer money. I'm still like shocked that they could get away with that. I know you're fighting it in court, and I fully expect it'll be unconstitutional in like 20 years whenever it makes its way through the court system. But could you just explain that?

Nick: Yes. So, I exposed California for all the fraud that they've enabled here inside the state. And they use what's called immigration support service providers, and it quite literally means anybody who provides services to illegal immigrants or immigrants. And that includes nonprofits and healthcare facilities.

So, actually today—this just happened literally today—I filmed all these daycares in San Diego, and when I exposed it, Newsom came after me. But today, they found 12 individuals who were all immigrants and they charged them with $10 million of fraud. That happened today.

Sacks: California did?

Nick: California, the DOJ did. So, underneath this new bill, this new law that they created, if these immigration support service providers were to give me a piece of paper saying, "Hey, you can't upload that video," I can't upload that video. And they only created that after I exposed the fraud.

Sacks: Wait, wait, wait. First of all, what is an—was it immigration support services? Like, what is that?

Nick: Yeah, it means legal services, healthcare facilities, quite literally anything where your tax dollars go to provide the services for illegal immigrants or immigrants here…

Sacks: …from the state of California. So the state of California is funding—

Nick: —these businesses, basically—

Sacks: —to provide services to illegals.

Nick: Yes. It can be medical. It can even be NGOs, nonprofits that received grants from the government. For instance, the people who sponsored this bill—it's called CHIRLA. They've received $80 million and they do the advocacy work for illegal immigrants here inside the United States.

Sacks: Wait, they got $80 million? Sorry, million or billion?

Nick: 80 million.

Sacks: Million? Nonprofit?

Nick: Nonprofit.

Sacks: And then, it sounds like the law is written that any service to immigrants—

Nick: Yeah, you can't go do this work, because they're trying to protect the community.

Sacks: So, wait, but how do they stop you? Let's say you go to one of these NGOs or businesses that's received this funding. You record it. And now they're saying you can't upload it?

Nick: Yeah. So, if they simply were enrolled in this service, then they give me a piece of paper saying, "Hey, you can't upload that video," a demand letter. I can't upload the video. And if I do, I'll get a $4,000 fine. And then I'll have to go to court and I'll have to pay for their legal fees if they win. So $4,000 is just the minimum if they have 10 employees in there who all are part of the service.

Sacks: Sorry, doesn't that violate your constitutional rights?

Nick: Yeah, First Amendment rights.

Sacks: And so, do you sue the state of California?

Nick: Yeah, I'm suing the state of California right now.

Sacks: To undo that bill?

Nick: Yes.

Jason: Ostensibly, by the way, Sacks, this was all under the pretext of our favorite term, "safety," because what Nick Shirley was doing in knocking on a door and saying, "Is this business open or closed?" was making people feel unsafe. And if you use that word "unsafe," well then everybody has to rally around it. And they literally called this the "Nick Shirley law." So I think this is the most amazing badge for you, and it's an award. The fact that they're creating laws to try to stop you from doing basic journalism means you're kicking fucking ass, Nick. Don't stop.

Chamath: These First Amendment cases though have been incredibly well litigated. So, do they just pass this knowing that it will probably get overturned at the federal level, and then it's up to you to raise the money, find the con-law people, and then take the case? Is that what it is? Or do they actually legitimately think there's legal standing? What does your team tell you about that law that's trying to stop you?

Nick: Yeah. I don't think they thought Nick Shirley would hear about this bill, cuz they called it AB2624. And unless an assemblyman dubbed it the "Stop Nick Shirley Act," I probably wouldn't have heard about it. So, California—they've pretty much passed all these laws. Like, it's called "Comifornia" for a reason. To get a bill passed in California in the legislature, there's 40 senators. 30 of them are Democrats. 10 of them are Republicans. It needs 21 votes to pass. So it's quite literally nearly almost impossible for a Republican to pass anything here inside the state of California.

Jason: Let's be clear, Gavin Newsom signed this.

Nick: Yeah.

Chamath: And who is the impetus of this bill? Like, is there a way that people are teasing out the funding cycle and the people that were behind this thing, or no?

Nick: Well, CHIRLA, they're the co-sponsor—but who received $80 million. The person who created this bill is the wife of the attorney general. Her name is Mia Bonta. So, meanwhile, the attorney general is supposed to prosecute the fraud. Well, his wife's creating laws to make it harder for fraud to be prosecuted and to go after and be exposed.

起源故事：一个 24 岁的 YouTuber 如何走到今天

Chamath: How did you start? Let's take a step back, Nick, for the folks that don't necessarily know the origin story. How did you stumble into this?

Nick: When I was 15 years old, I started making YouTube videos, vlogs, and pranks. As I got older, I got more interested to see what was actually happening in the world. But at that time, around 2020, you couldn't make videos with the word "Trump" in the title, or if you talked about politics or talked about COVID, you might be demonetized. So you couldn't make any money.

And so then I ended up taking like a 2-year break on a mission trip for our church and went to Santiago, Chile. I started learning about all these people that were fleeing Venezuela. They were going to Chile and they were telling me about how people are going to the United States.

So then I got back to the United States, my mom was also keeping up to date with that. And then when I got back home, I went to the southern border and I started interviewing people in Spanish saying like, "How'd you guys come over here? Like, what's going on?" And I thought it was super sad that all these people were coming over, fleeing the country. And then I get this lady's WhatsApp who was from Ecuador. She said she had no money at the border. And the next day she texted me saying she was in New York City. And I was like, "That's super strange."

And so, for the past 2 and a half years, I've been making a video every single week about something that's happening here inside the United States. And I went from 20,000 subscribers, nobody knowing me, to now having—I created one of the most viewed videos ever in internet history exposing the fraudsters in Minnesota. And I only knew about that fraud because I had been making a video every single week from across the world.

Chamath: What happens? Like, whistleblowers reach out to you and say, "Hey, Nick, go over here. Go over there"?

Nick: Yes. So I rely heavily upon the people in these states to let me know what's going on. Like, I'm pretty much—I made a joke—I'm like a congressman for the entire United States who actually listens to the people. But I don't work for anybody.

Jason: Well, and what I really appreciate about what you're doing is: man-on-the-street is a really challenging art form and journalistic format. It's incredibly brave for you to go out there, put yourself at risk. And, just to be clear so people can appreciate this: you have no formal journalistic training. You have learned everything on your own, and you have funded it. And I think it's important that we're clear about this because people make allegations, "Oh, you're a plant. Somebody's funding you." You're funded by the people through your X.com account. You make tens of thousands of dollars a month—I think maybe hundreds of thousands a year—just to sustain yourself.

Nick: Yeah. My whole goal was to make $300 a day in 2023. I thought I could do everything with $300 a day. I was like, "I'm going to be balling. That's $100,000 a year." And then I started making more and more money. I post this Minnesota fraud video—my mom literally films it, that's my favorite thing. People like, "Nick's a Fed." I'm like, would a Fed have his mom filming his YouTube videos when he's 24 years old?

Jason: Not a Fed thing to do.

Nick: Yeah. Not a Fed thing to do. I think they could find somebody better if that was the case. But I was just 100% working for myself to show people what was actually happening, and I've created a lot of change.

为什么部分观众讨厌他：Jason 的"洞见"

Chamath: The audience reaction is a little polarized, right? There are obviously people like us who are like—

Nick: You know, stealing is wrong.

Chamath: Then there's obviously fraudsters who can be angry at you.

Nick: Very angry.

Chamath: But then there are passive viewers that actually really dislike what you're doing.

Nick: Yeah. I don't understand.

Chamath: How do you unpack that? Like, why is that reaction happening?

Nick: Ultimately, I know what I'm doing is right. And for you to be defending a fraudster who opens up a learning center, I'm like, you might need to rethink something.

Jason: I can tell you what this is.

Nick: People say you're racist.

Jason: I can tell you what's happening here, Chamath. Having been a journalist and come up with these people—

Chamath: Oh, here we go.

Jason: No, no, it's actually super important.

Chamath: Jason lectures Nick.

Jason: It's not a lecture. It's an insight. And you're lucky to hear it. So sit back.

What you represent to them is a threat, because they came up and they wanted to do what you're doing. They were idealistic, these journalists, and they wanted to be brave enough to uncover these things—and they've become captured and politicized, and they have picked a side. You haven't.

That's why they criticize you. And the criticism they have of you is, "Oh, he wasn't fact-checking here. Wasn't thorough enough here." Okay, fine. On the margins, you're learning on the job. And I've had conversations with you privately about little nuances of things that you need to tighten up. None of that is important.

What's important is that you find fraud. You find actual real fraud, and you put the people on camera and you fucking shame them, and then they get arrested, and you're forcing the AGs in this country to face it. And it's just you. It's just you and your pure desire and energy to do it.

And that's what journalists hate about you—because they could do it too, and they should be ashamed that they don't. This was the job of 60 Minutes and Frontline, and they forgot how to do their job. And you're picking up the mantle of what Frontline and 60 Minutes used to be.

Nick: I agree. Give me some.

— Fuck yeah. — I die.

明尼苏达骗局：40 亿浏览与倒台的政客

Chamath: Are the AGs taking up the cases?

Nick: Well, I'll go expose it, and if they want to do something about it, I put all the information in the videos. And so, that's one thing I have seen—there actually has been change. They just found the 12 people today. The learners in Minnesota—most of them fled the country, I believe—but they got the head.

Chamath: Oh, is that right? So give us the quota actually about the daycares in Minnesota.

Nick: Yes. So the daycares in Minnesota—it was the craziest thing, because I was just sitting in my room. I just posted that video. I had no idea it was going to be like the biggest video ever. It got 4 billion views in 7 days, which was pretty insane.

So I post that video, and then there starts to be riots and protests. People start dying to cover for the learners. The politicians were incentivizing people to go out and riot because they knew like the ICE was there, but they could distract everyone by getting people out to the street to cover up for the fraud.

Well, it didn't really work, cuz Tim Walz dropped out of re-election in Minnesota. The head person of the learning centers who had received $4 million, she tried to go to London on a one-way ticket, and then she got caught for daycare fraud. And so she was the head—like the head honcho of the learners. She got caught. She got busted. Then the biggest autism bust of all time took place there as well. So, I've been very productive.

Chamath: So, wait—so did she get prosecuted?

Nick: Yes. And she plead guilty.

Chamath: She plead guilty?

Nick: Yeah.

Chamath: Oh, wow. And what's the sentence?

Nick: I don't know yet.

Chamath: Okay. Maybe it hasn't happened yet.

Nick: Yeah.

主流媒体去哪了

Chamath: Did you see Bill Gurley's presentation?

Nick: I watched a bit of it. It's kind of hard to hear back.

Chamath: Yeah. So, I mean, there's a point he was making, which is that journalists seem to have become selective in the stories that they're chasing and the investigations that they're doing, and there seems to be a reason that's this kind of politicized point.

What's your view? Have you met with journalists and talked with them? Have any of them reached out? And do you have a sense on what motivates them to say things, do things one way or not the other way?

Nick: No one from the mainstream has reached out to me to say like, "Hey, how are you doing this?" Instead, they investigate me, and they'll write hit pieces on me. I'm like, "Okay, like good for you."

Jason: Investigating the investigator. Yeah. That shows you exactly how threatened they are by you.

And I think where you are going to be—just having known you for one year and watching the improvements in the crispness—you are going to be so dangerous when you have a modest amount of resources. And I think what we really need to do is commit to making sure you have more funding.

And so, right after we get on here, I'm going to subscribe and I'm going to put in, you know, whatever, a couple thousand dollars a month to support you. And I think everybody here should. You're doing great work. You need to have some researchers on the team. You need to have some backup. And you need to have security, because what you're doing is truly a threat to criminals and the mob has always wanted—

Nick: No, I'll take it.

Chamath: What was that? What was it?

Chamath: You were the son that Jason has always wanted.

Jason: No, no. I mean, I have three great daughters. But I'm just—you're what I got in when I got into journalism. What you're doing is why I got into it, which was the role of journalism. And I think Bill Gurley pointed it out so well in his talk, which was: there are still great investigative journalists out there, there just aren't enough of them. And I think it's fantastic that there's a new generation doing this, and that you're doing.

新一代调查者的崛起：X 平台的角色

Chamath: So there have been a few others that have emerged since you came out. Minnesota piece was such a big maybe inspiration, but it was also a beacon to a lot of people like, "Oh, we can go do this like you did." Are you seeing more of this? Do you think that they're being successful? And what do you think's changing?

Nick: Yeah, I think a lot of people are taking it up, and they're seeing—like, with X, if it wasn't for Elon and X, none of this would have been possible. For instance, I post that video about the fraud on YouTube—it does well, it gets a few million views. On X, it got 140 million views. And the most important people in the world see it and they're able to see like, "Oh, we're not doing our job. Let's go do what needs to be done." Like, the government, I caught them kind of backhanded on that. So they had to go step in.

But I do think a lot of individuals—like, I do hope I am motivating a lot of kids, especially my generation, to be less of a complainer and be more of a doer. And I think journalism, people think of it as just showing what's going on. Well, you can actually create massive change inside of the country in the areas that you live in. That's something that I've seen with my journalism. I'm not just playing defense. I'm actually going out showing people what's going on, and I'm not just leaving the story after it's done. Like, I'm continuing to follow through, because if it's real corruption, like, it needs to be taken down, right?

Chamath: And what other people don't realize—because you became I think pretty famous from the Minnesota video, but you had other stuff before where it wasn't about chasing down corruption. Like, you went into the favelas in Brazil, right? Which was incredibly scary. And you've done a lot of this stuff. Are you still doing those sorts of things, or is everything now about government corruption?

Nick: I would love to continue to do those videos, and I will do more. These past 8 months, every morning I'm waking up to something new about fraud and corruption. So I've kind of just been spearheading that. But I would like to get more into that stuff.

Like, I almost got kidnapped in the Brazilian favelas. I met up with the head of Comando Vermelho inside this favela in Rio de Janeiro. And literally, there's only a few things that could have happened with me and him and this broken-down shack at the top of the favela.

Got also nearly taken hostage in Cuba. A two-star communist general came down to try and figure out why I was in Cuba and why I was leaving early. So, that stuff's still super important. The fraud stuff's just kind of taken over my life recently, though.

下一个战场：福利欺诈

Chamath: What are the other big pockets of fraud that you are scratching at that you think exist? The big honeypots that you're going to go chase down and uncover?

Nick: Welfare fraud here inside the United States is just absolutely insane. Like, all of it.

Chamath: Can you explain that?

Nick: For instance, food stamps. There's a strip club in Portland, Oregon, where you can use your SNAP card. Like, the government, especially underneath Biden, they literally let open like the floodgates to fraud. I mean, Tim Walz was celebrating and using the daycares in his debates against JD Vance, right?

So all these social benefit programs have literally been looted—whether it be SNAP, whether it be daycares, whether it be adult daycares—like literally, you name it: hospices, all these things that have received government money are just full of fraud.

Chamath: And so now you're just trying to pull the thread and uncover as much of it as possible?

Nick: Yeah. And it's hard now, cuz I have to have security. Like, people literally want to kill me. And so I have to be super strategic in what's going to stop a fraudster from me knocking on his door and him realizing that his time's up and just shooting me so the video doesn't get posted. That's stuff I think about when I go to bed. Like, how do I go out and make these videos a bit differently?

Chamath: Well, are there different ways that you can get the information you need to tell the story without actually having to confront the person in real time?

Nick: Yeah, people want to see the person get confronted.

Chamath: So, I mean, but this is what's so interesting—because what you're talking about is like at the end of the day, you're still fighting the attention mechanism that you live under. Your incentive is to tell the truth, but there's a last point where your incentive is: I must do something that will get views as well.

Nick: Yeah. That's how all this stuff happens.

Jason: Well, you know, 60 Minutes as an example does undercover reporting and always has, and they would—if a subject would not come on 60 Minutes, they would go to their home and wait for them outside their office and home to confront them and ask those questions. They would tell them they're going to do it. So, I think you're well within your right to do that.

I think as you professionalize your operation—and it's incredibly brave what you're doing—I think you have to ask for a bit more support from the audience. And right now you can do a $5 subscription, but you should also ask people to be charter supporters, you know, at a $500 level, $1,000 level, like Substack might allow you to do. And I think you should be very aggressive in asking for more support, because the government—we heard from Vice President J.D. Vance—10, 20% of our tax dollars are being wasted. If we support you to do this work, get a researcher, get an extra video editor—you just need about three or four people around you to support you—and this is really going to take off.

If you have those three or four people, we're all going to save more money. And we need to, as a country, get behind you and say: people who are stealing from the government—they should carry double the sentence, because you're stealing from the actual society, right? And I don't care what country, it doesn't matter what state it is, immigrant or American, and they've been here. You're stealing from the actual country that is giving you, you know, the protection of living in these United States. It is really sinister to steal from the country. It really is.

And I'm really upset that you are faced with security issues and a lack of support and this criticism on the ticky-tacky things. Do not stop doing what you're doing.

Nick: Thank you very much.

结语：合法的浪费也是一种腐败

Nick: And if we can stop fraud, we can literally save the country. That's something people don't understand. What's crazy is—it's not just fraud. I think the California high-speed rail project—anyone can look at that objectively and say that is the most insane thing on earth. Why are we doing this? $240 billion to go from Fresno to Modesto at three times the price of an airplane ticket. None of it makes sense. Literally, none of it makes sense. And the guy got paid half a billion for non-work.

Chamath: It's a billionaire in Italy who got paid that money.

Nick: I tricked him.

Chamath: How much did he get paid?

Nick: Half a billion.

Chamath: Say half a billion.

Nick: Did you watch the video?

Chamath: Yeah. So, after I saw that video—so Nick sent me that video and then I traced down who got paid that half billion, and the ultimate owner is a billionaire in Italy.

Nick: I didn't know that.

Chamath: And the whole story when you kind of dig into this—so this isn't fraud. It's legal.

Nick: Mhm.

Chamath: It's a legal system. It's a legal system, and I think it falls under that idea of waste or some sort of corruption. But I think it is as—the fraud stuff anyone can get behind. But this is the stuff—

Nick: Unethical and illogical.

Chamath: There's complacency, there's corruption, there's unaccountability, and these are the things that just trickled into this massive waterfall that we're drowning in right now. And I think it's really important what you're doing, and I think on behalf of a lot of people, I really appreciate the mission you're on. You're an incredible person. We thank you for the work.

Nick: Thank you guys so much. Thanks for being—

Chamath: No problem. I appreciate it.

— Fuck yeah. — Thanks, brother. Appreciate it. — Thank you. Great job. — Thanks, Jason. Appreciate it.

## 一、"高铁到无处"是一面照妖镜：它照出的不是无能，而是激励结构的完美运行
大多数人看加州高铁的第一反应是"政府真蠢"。但一个更令人不安的观察是：**从系统内部人员的激励来看，这个项目运行得极其"成功"**。
- 承包商每天不工作赚 17 万美元，一个月 500 万，最近一次"延误赔偿"和解金额是 5 亿美元——**"不干活"比"干活"利润率更高**。 - 加州至今没买真正的列车。视频中 Nick 的解读很尖锐："因为他们自己也知道永远不会有火车跑在这条铁轨上。" - 每年 10 亿美元的稳定拨款，是**一个持续 20 年的现金流机器**，它对既得利益者而言不是失败，是"年金"。
系统的荒谬只在"这是为了修一条铁路"这个前提下才成立。**一旦你把它重新定义为"一个把公共资金稳定转移给特定承包商的合法管道"，一切参数——工期、预算、变更单——都变得完全合理**。这正是经济学家 Mancur Olson 在《国家兴衰探源》里说的"分利联盟"：项目越大越难完成，越能维持越多人的饭碗，因此"完不成"才是均衡解。
## 二、跨领域连接：加州高铁 = 一个"反向 SpaceX"，它的失
